#5764. People and Vertical AI: The responsible and trusted framework for energy and water

Where AI in energy and water goes next and the principles that should guide it

I have always held a simple conviction — energy and water utilities should not be spectators to the AI transformation of their own industry. They should shape it, together with the partners and technologists building alongside them.

That conviction matters because few industries carry the weight that energy and water do. They are the services every other part of modern life is built on — be it homes, hospitals, schools, businesses, data centers and increasingly, the AI economy itself. When they work, they are invisible. When they fail, everything else stops. Their success is measured in three outcomes the public feels directly: affordability, reliability and trust.

Rising energy costs, extreme weather, electrification and the growing demand from large loads are putting these outcomes under increasing pressure. At the same time, utilities are being asked to modernize operations, make better use of data and respond faster to changing customer and grid demands.

This is changing the conversation around AI. The question is no longer simply what AI can do, but where it can deliver value, how much autonomy it should have and what safeguards must govern its use.

At this year's WE3 Global AI Summit, conversations among energy and utility leaders reflected this shift. As AI moves from individual applications into customer, workforce, business and grid operations, the industry must think beyond capability to the conditions under which AI can be trusted to act.

My belief is that the answer lies in People + Vertical AI: an approach that combines industry-specific intelligence with human experience, judgment and accountability. Vertical AI brings the data, domain knowledge and operational context required to work within the realities of energy and water. People establish its purpose, define its boundaries and remain accountable for its outcomes. Four principles should guide this approach.

The relationship between customers and the grid is changing. For decades, customer service and grid operations largely functioned as separate domains. Electric vehicles, rooftop solar, battery storage and smart thermostats are increasingly connecting them. A customer's electric vehicle can become a flexible grid resource. A utility interaction about energy usage or payments can open the door to demand response and affordability programs.

This creates an opportunity for utilities to coordinate flexible demand across homes and businesses, manage peak consumption and make better use of distributed energy resources. When designed well, these programs can help defer infrastructure investments, improve grid flexibility and manage costs. But technology alone will not make this possible. Customers need clear choices, fair incentives and confidence in how their data and participation are used.

Utilities will increasingly need to manage the grid with their customers, not simply deliver services to them. Vertical AI must therefore connect the customer experience with grid intelligence, bringing these traditionally separate functions into a more coordinated operating model.

In energy and water, intelligence is not just a model. It depends on people, processes, data and security working together. When these elements remain disconnected, AI has a narrower view of utility operations and a weaker foundation for sound decisions. Yet customer, workforce, business and grid operations continue to rely on systems and data that were often designed independently. The result is fragmented information, disconnected workflows and limited visibility across the ecosystem.

This is why the real unit of value in Vertical AI is the connected workflow and this is where depth of industry data becomes decisive. It requires intelligence grounded in the industry's operating context, including utility-specific data, processes, regulatory requirements and historical interactions.

With more than 15 years of experience building Vertical AI for energy and water, we have seen how important this industry context is. Our work at SEW.AI, drawing on more than 4.3 trillion data points across energy and water usage, customer interactions and utility operations. That depth is what allows it to reason across all four domains with genuine context, connecting the systems utilities already run without replacing them.

Agentic AI moves intelligence from recommendation to execution: systems that can reason through complex, multi-step processes and carry them through to resolution.

In utilities, however, action demands specialization. A general-purpose agent can follow instructions, but it cannot be expected to grasp the regulatory, operational and safety consequences of its actions. Vertical agents start from a different premise. Each is purpose-designed for a specific domain, such as outage response, field dispatch, payments or customer care. Each is trained on industry data and governed by industry rules. Together they are orchestrated so that each hands off seamlessly to the next. What emerges is less a single intelligence than a coordinated team of specialists.

As distributed energy resources multiply and operational demands become more interconnected, this coordination will become increasingly important. Specialized agents can handle routine, repeatable tasks with greater consistency and speed, allowing utility employees to focus on exceptions, complex decisions and situations that require human judgment. The objective is not to automate every decision. It is to ensure that the right decisions are made with the right context, at the right time and that actions remain within clearly established boundaries.

The fourth principle underpins everything else: trust. And trust begins with security.

In energy and water, security is not an IT concern. It is a matter of public safety. Every AI agent introduced into a utility is a new identity with access to customer data, operational systems and, increasingly, physical infrastructure.

Security therefore cannot be layered on after deployment. It must be intrinsic — with verified identities, least-privilege access, auditable actions, appropriate data protection and clear escalation paths. Decisions with significant safety, financial or operational consequences require controls proportionate to their risk, including human approval where necessary. Governance must also extend beyond deployment. Utilities need visibility into how AI systems operate, the permissions they exercise, the decisions they influence and the circumstances in which they must escalate to people.

Governance of this kind is not a brake on innovation. It is what allows autonomy to scale responsibly, earned workflow by workflow, with accountability that always remains human. Regulators, boards and communities will hold utilities, not algorithms, responsible for every outcome.

Vertical AI brings industry knowledge, speed and scale. People bring experience, judgment and accountability. Neither is sufficient on its own.

The energy and water industries have navigated major transitions before, from electrification to digitization. Each required more than new technology. It required changes in how organizations operated, how people worked and how services were delivered to communities.

AI will demand the same discipline. Its progress should not be measured by how many decisions can be automated or how much autonomy a system can achieve. It should be measured by whether utilities can use it responsibly to make essential services more affordable, more reliable and more trusted.

That is the standard we should hold ourselves to as an industry. And it is the principle behind the People + Vertical AI approach we continue to advance.

SEW.AI is the global Vertical AI Platform purpose-built for the energy and utility industry, enabling organizations to transform customer engagement, workforce productivity, business operations and grid intelligence through the People + Vertical AI framework.

#5763. US to install 36% more wind turbines in 2025 than previous year

The United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S. Wind Energy Monitor” report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

Amid a challenging market environment, the report shows that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of new wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts. However, timing has shifted, as 2026 and 2027 will deliver significant gains, at 10.7 GW and 12.7 GW, respectively, as more assets advance through the development pipeline.

While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity. This back-loaded installation pattern is consistent with typical project-commissioning timelines.

U.S. turbine order intake has rebounded to pre-One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) levels quarter-over-quarter, supported by 2+ GW of firm commitments in Q3, the biggest intake in the region in the last nine months and a 79% quarter-over-quarter increase. However, true visibility remains limited as OEMs increasingly withhold project details and much qualifying “start-of-construction” activity occurs through off-site component manufacturing.

The market will then see a noticeable drop off, as 2029 weakens meaningfully quarter-over-quarter following project cancellations and inactive designations for late-decade capacity, driven by permitting and broader development challenges.

“The U.S. power market is facing mounting strain after a decade of flat demand, with utilities committing to 160 GW of large-load additions. This represents a significant opportunity for wind energy, which benefits from strengthened economic fundamentals and a compelling business case driven by its competitively low LCOE,” said Leila Garcia da Fonseca, director of research at Wood Mackenzie. “However, turbine costs remain elevated due to tariffs and mid-term wind growth will depend on resolving permitting and policy uncertainty.”

Power demand growth through 2029 is expected to average around 3% compared to just 0.7% over the previous decade, with data centers accounting for approximately 59 GW of the 90 GW total peak demand growth. This surge in baseload demand positions wind as a natural fit to meet rising power needs.

The five-year capacity outlook remains unchanged at 39.8 GW of added capacity quarter-over-quarter. The 2025-2027 pipeline is fully committed with all projects having turbine orders in place. More than 60% of the three-year capacity outlook has been commissioned or is under construction.

Activity is led by western states, such as Wyoming, New Mexico and others, that will account for 34% of activity in this time period. Major projects driving the outlook include Pattern’s 3.5-GW SunZia project in New Mexico, which will position the developer as 2026’s top installer, and Invenergy’s 998-MW Towner Energy Center in Colorado, the largest single project expected in 2027.

The market continues expanding geographically, with Arkansas bringing its first utility-scale onshore wind project online through Cordelio’s Crossover Wind.

The repowering market remains strong, as Wood Mackenzie projects that 18 projects will drive 2.5 GW of capacity additions in the next three years.

Wood Mackenzie expects the offshore installation pace to slow in Q4 2025 due to harsh winter weather conditions, pushing remaining capacity into 2026. Despite these near-term adjustments, Vineyard Wind has demonstrated strong execution, connecting 15 turbines in Q3 and delivering 200 GWh through nine months.

“U.S. offshore wind shows diverging momentum,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Projects under construction with COD estimated for 2026 continue to hit key milestones, but post-2027 developments face potential delays amid constrained wind turbine installation vessel capacity, driving delays and contract terminations.”

The offshore sector is also experiencing significant financial pressure.

The report highlights that uncertainty around tariffs is a threat to projections. Wood Mackenzie projects that tariffs will drive up turbine costs in 2026, before moderating in subsequent years. In total, U.S. onshore wind capex is projected to increase by 5% through 2029.

“U.S. wind turbine pricing is experiencing unprecedented uncertainty as conflicting market and regulatory forces interact,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Domestic manufacturing overcapacity relative to permitted project volumes, particularly after 2028, would normally place downward pressure on prices. Despite this, onshore wind costs are expected to continue rising due to tariff exposure on raw material inputs and subcomponents.”

#5762. 10 Reasons for the Big Blue Wave

I wrote the other day about a top reason US voters said they voted for Democrats in such large numbers — corruption in the Trump household, Trump administration, and Republican Party. It was surprising to me that this showed up as the biggest factor for so many people … even though it was also a huge one for me. However, I think everyone knows what the most significant reason was for the dramatic, historic shift in voting. It’s the economy, stupid! That’s the famous old quote from James Carville, a political strategist working for Bill Clinton when he was running for president in 1992, and it’s as relevant as ever. With that in mind, let’s take a look at some of the top reasons for the Big Blue Wave.

Inflation has hit and hit and hit. Donald Trump said while campaigning for president in 2024, “Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again.” However, of course, beyond the fact that he didn’t come close to doing that and was just making an obviously false promise, Trump actually jacked up inflation significantly with his obsessive, high tariffs and with his war on Iran. Whereas it’s often hard to tie inflation to a specific presidential policy, in this case, we had two specific presidential policies that clearly caused inflation! Even when there are no clear links, voters blame the president for such matters, so imagine how much they must have done so in this case!

Aside from inflation, the economy overall isn’t great. The country isn’t adding a bunch of jobs, wages and salaries aren’t rising much, and people by and large don’t feel optimistic about their financial futures. So, combined with quickly rising costs, a very meh economy had voters wanting change.

As already discussed at length, voters were fed up with corruption in the Republican Party. As some CleanTechnica readers pointed out, if people were prospering financially and not being hit with severe inflation, many of them probably wouldn’t care about the corruption. However, when considering #1 and #2, people naturally get quite frustrated with blatant corruption and essentially high-volume robbery from Donald Trump, the Trump family, Trump staffers, and the Republican Party broadly.

Naturally, this is heavily linked to #1, since it is largely this war that has led to gas prices rising so much. However, also more broadly, Americans are fed up with forever wars in the Middle East, there’s never been a good and strong case for why Trump started this war (as tends to be the case with these wars in the Middle East), and many people really don’t like seeing innocent schoolchildren being bombed to death. Trump was supposed to be an anti-war president (I know that many people believed that, even though Trump is a naturally aggressive, violent person who seemed to me like someone who would obviously get into wars). Voters who cared a lot about this topic might have felt betrayed by Trump and swung strongly away from him and the Republican Party (which has a tendency to get us into these oil wars in the Middle East).

Even for many people who thought we needed stronger actions to stop people from coming to the United States, the inhumane, deadly, Gestapo-like ICE army — often including violent people with their faces covered and without ID acting like the mafia — was a step or ten too far. There are countless stories of good, innocent people being jailed without cause, or even murdered, by this Nazi-like police force. There was clearly a huge blue shift in certain places as a result of this.

Many voters have gotten extremely concerned about Republicans under Trump’s leadership eroding the foundations of our democracy. While this became a major problem in Trump’s first term, he has gone much further in his second term. Apparently, more people have woken up to this problem and it has freaked them out.

A massive rollout of AI and data centers — often feeling completely forced on us — has upset a lot of Americans. This does come back to #1, too. Giant data centers have jacked up electricity prices a ton in several regions. Others are threatened with the same thing happening. The same thing has also happened from the crypto craze, which more and more people have also found to be a scam. Seeing billions upon billions trillions of dollars funneled toward AI companies while people are struggling, and then seeing electricity prices rising significantly — surprise, surprise — pisses people off and makes them vote for change.

No matter how you cut it, people vote based on money — in particular, their own money. Whether it’s food prices, gas prices, electricity prices, clothing prices, doll prices, computer prices, car prices, or other prices, people don’t like it when they have to pay a lot more money for stuff — especially when they aren’t making much more money, or more money at all. Simply put, this matter deserves extra weight, because the critical thing swing voters are often voting on is just that — money.

Of course, there are solar, wind, and EV aspects to all of this. Trump has made the US spend a fortune to stop wind and solar farms from providing the US with cheap electricity, and he has made the US spend a fortune keeping old, dirty coal power plants open. High gas prices have also pushed people to buy electric cars, but mostly in other countries where there’s more EV choice and more people have more sense on this topic. However, by and large, I don’t think American voters really shifted much based on Trump stopping renewable energy projects, promoting coal and gas, or limiting EV choice in the United States. People voting for Democrats on climate and cleantech matters were already voting for Democrats based on these issues. It’s unlikely many people at all shifted from red to blue because of these factors.

#5761. Over court objections, DOE issues 7th order to keep Michigan coal plant online

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Environmental groups say they are “evaluating all legal options” after a federal appeals court vacated a previous order for the same plant, ruling DOE exceeded its authority.

Utility Dive reported in June that Campbell was operating at a capacity factor of 46.1%, down from a nearly 66% average in the same periods in the previous four years.

Environmental and consumer advocates say there is no energy emergency requiring the plant to remain online, and forcing it to stay active has already saddled consumers with excess costs.

Consumers spent $303 million through the end of September to operate the plant under DOE emergency orders after accounting for $344 million in market revenues, according to its quarterly filing.

Consumers spokesperson Brian Wheeler said the utility “will continue to follow the law and operate our Campbell plant,” and that “consistent with these emergency orders, we will work to ensure that everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.”

“Someone will be left holding the financial bag,” ELPC CEO Howard Learner said in a statement. And following the appeals court decision, the “latest purported emergency order is likewise illegal.”

“DOE should just stop issuing these orders and stop the meter from running up costs,” he said.

DOE did not immediately respond to questions about the new order and what may happen next.

The latest order will keep the 1,420-MW plant online another 90 days, until mid-February, bringing the total extension to more than 20 months, according to the Environmental Defense Fund.

Meanwhile, Consumers is seeking to recover “ballooning costs” from ratepayers in 11 states, EDF said: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Wisconsin.

Campbell “illustrates the enormous price tag attached to keeping these uneconomic coal plants on life support for months on end,” Ted Kelly, EDF director and lead counsel for U.S. clean energy, said in a statement. “These are completely unnecessary costs, yet families and businesses that are already stretched thin are being asked to foot the bill.”

According to DOE, coal plants across the U.S. “are being saved from premature retirement,” and in 2025 more than 17 GW of coal-fired electricity generation was preserved.

The J.H. Campbell power plant had been set to retire in May 2025. Ensuring Campbell and other coal plants are available to operate “has prevented blackouts and likely saved lives,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in DOE’s latest announcement.

The emergency conditions that led to the issuance of the original order persist, the agency said, and a joint report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation and NERC’s Regional Entities “highlights how events that occurred during the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period, including Winter Storm Fern, demonstrated the need for dispatchable generation capacity from facilities like the Campbell Plant.”

According to EDF, since May 2025 the Trump administration has “repeatedly extended emergency orders to keep six coal plants online beyond retirement, even as those plants have racked up around $600 million in losses.”

“Of the unlawfully extended coal plants, the Campbell plant in Michigan has emitted the most health-harming air pollution,” it added.

According to the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, DOE’s latest order to keep Campbell open “will eat away at more than half of the $600 million the plant’s closure was set to save Michiganders by 2040.”

Consumers in Michigan “deserve affordable energy and relief from rising costs — not executive overreach that forces families to subsidize aging, expensive fossil fuel infrastructure,” Bentley Johnson, federal government affairs director for Michigan LCV, said in a statement.

#5760. Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs

This analysis of eight residential programs shows that, if properly implemented, cities can use a new organics collection program to build a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable solid waste system.

Residential curbside organics collection is expanding across the United States as states and local governments seek to reduce food waste sent to landfills and incinerators, meet waste diversion and climate goals, and respond to landfill capacity constraints. Yet for many communities, the perceived cost of adding organics recycling collection atop existing trash and recycling collection remains a significant barrier to implementation.

NRDC’s Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs report finds that there is no single predetermined cost of implementing and operating an organics collection program. The cost to communities depends substantially on how organics collection is designed and, critically, how it is integrated into the broader solid waste system. A municipality that simply adds weekly organics collection to an otherwise unchanged garbage and recycling program is likely to see an increase in cost. However, a municipality that uses the introduction of organics to evaluate and optimize collection frequency, routes, contracts, processing arrangements, participation, and funding can offset a significant portion of the new service cost. In fact, with deliberate planning and system-wide optimization, curbside organics can serve not simply as an added service but as a catalyst for a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable solid waste system.

This analysis draws on eight established residential curbside organics programs and two active pilot programs representing communities of different sizes, densities, regions, service models, and participation structures. Across these communities, several findings emerge:

The community comparisons demonstrate the practical significance of these choices. In several communities that were studied, residents receive garbage, recycling, and organics collection at rates that are comparable to what residents in peer communities pay for garbage and recycling alone. For example, in Austin, Texas, residents pay approximately $29 per month for three-stream curbside service, compared with approximately $22 per month for garbage and recycling service in Raleigh, North Carolina. The comparison is not intended to suggest that every community can replicate a particular rate; rather, it demonstrates that the addition of organics does not necessarily translate into a proportionate increase in the total cost of residential solid waste service.

The Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs report aims to support states and local communities in implementing effective strategies to fund residential curbside organic waste collection programs as a critical tool to improving resilience, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and diverting material from landfills and incinerators. The central implication for local governments is therefore straightforward: The affordability of curbside organics is largely a program design question. Communities considering organics collection can begin by evaluating the economics and performance of their existing solid waste system; identifying efficiencies that can help offset the new service; testing critical assumptions through a pilot, where appropriate; and finally, designing a full-scale program around the participation, collection, processing, and funding structures that best fit local conditions. To support this process, the report translates these findings into a three-phase implementation framework for evaluating the existing system, designing and testing an organics program, and moving toward financially sustainable full-scale implementation.

By Anya Obrez, Advocacy Associate, Food Waste, Nature, NRDC, and Darby Hoover, Senior Resource Specialist, Environmental Health & Nature, NRDC.

#5759. FERC’s See on large loads, Western markets and affordability

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

FERC’s Lindsay See on federal permitting reform: “I think one of the biggest drivers in terms of cost and extra time is uncertainty in legal statutes.”

Lindsay See, a member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission since mid-2024, has been a leader on the agency’s permitting reform initiatives and has joined other commissioners in pushing transmission owners to use grid-enhancing technologies. Utility Dive met with See on Wednesday at the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners’ annual meeting in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Before joining FERC, See served as West Virginia’s solicitor general, where she successfully argued a case at the U.S. Supreme Court challenging greenhouse gas rules for power plants.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

LINDSAY SEE: I find NARUC really valuable because I am a former state attorney myself. I worked for the West Virginia [attorney general’s] office. I firmly believe in the importance of state and local solutions, and I think that's what I want to say to the states.

But primarily, it's what I want to hear from the states because I think we have so many issues where we have jurisdiction at FERC, and the states do, [too,] and I want to make sure that we're pulling in the same direction. So that's a lot of my message: How do we keep lines of communication open so they have the information they need from us, and vice versa.

I want to learn the different ways that states are approaching affordability issues, large-load challenge issues, how we can help at FERC. Some of what we're looking at is, how do we make sure that a lot of these new regulatory pushes and policies we have don't have unintended consequences.

They want more transparency, especially when it's coming to affordability issues. How do we make sure that they have the same information that we have so that they can do their job better when it comes to allocating retail rates? Particularly when it comes to large-load integration, there's been some blind spots on the state side in terms of which customers on the transmission side are driving those costs.

Even just a few years ago, when I worked in West Virginia, we didn't talk about PJM that much. Now we have regular ratepayers who are not energy nerds who are reading about PJM on the front page of the news and are seeing their bills go higher. So I think we're seeing a lot more pressure on what we're doing to understand, what do we have responsibility over, what don't we? That kind of public conversation is really different, but really helpful because it puts a really important focus for us to make sure that we have a clear sense of what we can control and what we can't control.

We've got a few buckets that we're really focused on. One is — especially when it comes to large-load integration and the show cause orders we have — how do we have transmission cost agreements that are clear about which customers are driving those costs to make sure that they're the ones who are paying their share and we're not saddling existing customers with those costs or with the risk of stranded investment.

In order to meet this incredible opportunity we have from large-load growth as a country, it's going to take new transmission investment that's absolutely required and it's necessarily expensive. So I think it's even more important for us to make sure that we are making the right sort of investments into the system.

In those show-cause orders, we focused on requiring transmission owners to consider alternative transmission technologies — to say, how can we do more with the existing system. I'm really focused on pushing as far as we can within our statutory structure because I understand we need new wires. But I want to make sure we've got the right incentives in place to use what we already have really well.

We need more infrastructure, both on the transmission side and on the pipeline side, so how do we make that permitting process as efficient and streamlined as possible? Because reducing that time and the legal uncertainty also has a direct cost consequence in terms of the amount of money those projects ultimately cost. So that is something within our control in areas where we've got permitting authority.

We see so much of the electricity sector that's powered by natural gas, being able to get that fuel where it needs to be at the right time is critical in order to have a reliable and affordable electricity sector, too. So the way I look at it is, everything that we can do to encourage a more efficient, streamlined, legally durable permitting process on the gas side has direct consequences on the power side, too.

I hear those concerns. I take them seriously. I, probably unsurprisingly, disagree with them. We do have really important environmental responsibilities, [and] I think it matters for us to fulfill those, but also not to go further than what the statutes require. And so I think some of the work that we've been doing over the past year and just in the past month, announcing a new draft policy statement, is really trying to be clear about where that line of what we're required to do begins and ends.

[The National Environmental Policy Act] is a statute that affirmatively requires us to create evidence in terms of the environmental record, but it doesn't require particular types of evidence.

So when we come to air modeling, for instance … my view is, we're not the environmental regulators and experts. EPA and the states are already doing a lot of that work, so we should be able to take advantage of the good work they're doing. There's other evidence that is not so time-intensive and kind of fraught with legal uncertainty and vulnerability that lets us do our particular job.

When anyone is putting information in the record, we are still required to consider that in the public interest. So we're not turning a blind eye to those concerns at all. This is just about what particular evidence we are specifically required to create. So I think not having redundancies in terms of what other agencies do, it doesn't take away from our responsibilities.

I am strongly supportive of permitting reform. I'm a former litigator. I lived in the trenches here. I think one of the biggest drivers in terms of cost and extra time is uncertainty in legal statutes when it comes to either agencies taking more time than they might need to to cover their bases. And then, of course, the time it takes in court, and if the agency loses and remands, we have to start over. That just adds so much in terms of time we, frankly, don't have to build out the system and [adds] cost to consumers.

We've been taking stock internally if this becomes law. There are huge responsibilities that FERC has in the bill, so we're trying to gear up and come up with a plan for how to do that.

PJM has significant challenges ahead. This is not a normal demand spike that we're seeing. The market was not designed for the circumstances we have with such large-load growth. And some of the PJM states are at the epicenter of data center growth.

We are seeing some reforms coming that are really targeted and focused on these urgent needs, but I think one of the things — and these are conversations I've had with PJM, and I know my colleagues have, too —  is how do we make sure it's not just playing whack-a-mole? And being able to have a vision for the future. I think the confidence piece for all market participants is so critical right now.

I think that loops back to some of the ongoing conversations about governance at PJM. We had a technical conference a few months ago where all the commissioners focused on this issue, and we're about to be getting some proposals. [The governance] issue matters a lot because in order for PJM to be nimble to respond to these concerns and to have the public's confidence, I think the governance piece is so critical to unlock the ability to move forward on some of these other substantive areas.

They get to make those decisions, and we support the choices they make. I spent a good amount of time out West last spring, and I was really encouraged to see those really collegial and thoughtful conversations in the West. They are watching very closely what's happening in the Eastern markets, too, to see what's working and what's not.

[The difficulties in PJM,] I think it's galvanizing the states out West to make sure that they're setting the right governance structures in place from the beginning that protect their voice and their interests. That's something I'm watching really closely on PJM market reform … what does it look like to have increased state involvement in the decision-making process that also corresponds to their increased responsibility for the regional issues?

I think about it in two ways. First, FERC is a creature of statute. We have our statutory mission. Permitting reform might change that, but the midterms don't. It's business as usual in that sense.

But the midterms definitely drive home how much Americans are concerned about the cost of living and about their energy bills specifically, and that goes to the heart of our mission for reliable and affordable energy. So I look at that, and I take that concern to heart. If anything, it puts a renewed focus and onus on us to make sure that when it comes to those areas within our control, we are really taking a hard look at what we can be doing.

#5758. Who Can Weather the Health Storm?

States facing the greatest health damage from climate change are the least equipped to protect their residents.

Across the United States, climate change is intensifying extreme weather events, resulting in escalating public health harms and severe economic damage. For example, devastating inland flooding in Texas in 2025 killed 134 people and damaged $1 billion worth of residential property; 2025’s catastrophic wildfires in Southern California destroyed more than 10,000 buildings (at a cost of $63 billion) and triggered more than 8,000 health-care visits; and Hurricane Milton’s 2024 landfall in Florida killed 32 people and damaged $34 billion in property. These climate costs are typically borne by disaster victims, insurers, state agencies, and the federal government. Given the retreat of federal leadership from climate policy, state governments are increasingly looking to improve preparedness and resiliency in order to reduce future costs and health impacts.

However, a new analysis led by NRDC and published in the journal Health Affairs sheds light on key state-level gaps between climate change–linked health damage and levels of preparedness. We find that some of the most climate-burdened states are the least equipped to help their residents recover from climate disasters and prepare for future dangers. The intersection of escalating climate risks and adaptation vulnerabilities demands state policy intervention. Better integrating social protection policies into state climate resiliency plans can help states close these gaps and better safeguard their residents.

By Dr. Vijay Limaye; Director, Applied Research Initiatives, Science Office & International, NRDC

#5757. NRG to sell 4.9 GW of gas plants to LS Power for $4B

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

NRG Energy CEO Robert Gaudette said the sale values one 1.2-GW Texas gas plant at $1,400/kW, while NRG is “developing 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation in Texas” for just above $1,000/kW.

NRG Energy has agreed to sell around 4.9 GW of gas plant capacity to LS Power, which approached NRG with an unsolicited offer of $4 billion — around eight times the plants’ annual adjusted EBITDA of $500 million, NRG President and CEO Robert Gaudette said during a Nov. 9 earnings call.

NRG plans for that $4 billion to go toward a $1 billion stock buyback and $2 billion debt reduction, with the remaining $1 billion providing “flexibility to reinvest in our long-term strategy through attractive contracted growth opportunities or further reduce debt,” Gaudette said. “We expect the sale to close in the second quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.”

“One aspect of the valuation worth highlighting is Jack County, which carries an implied value of approximately $1,400/KW,” Gaudette said. “For perspective, we're developing 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation in Texas for just above $1,000/KW. That comparison demonstrates the value we're realizing from selected existing assets while developing newer, more efficient generation at a lower cost.”

Gaudette said that NRG’s project of building a 1.2-GW combined-cycle natural gas-fired power plant in Texas to power the data center project of an unnamed cloud and AI hyperscaler is “on track, and I fully expect approved agreements and an announcement by year-end.”

“We're also advancing additional project opportunities with the same customer beyond the initial 1.2 GW,” he added. “Beyond the initial project, our pipeline of opportunities exceeds the turbine allocations and [engineering, procurement, and construction] capacity under our original development agreement with GE Vernova and Kiewit.”

That development agreement is for 5.4 GW of turbine capacity, according to NRG’s earnings presentation.

In response to an analyst question about whether the results of the recent midterm elections present any risks to the 1.2-GW project, Gaudette said, “The political environment has actually strengthened this project and our projects.”

“The way that we've gone about developing generation to support data centers and this large load growth over time, the political environment is where we thought it would always be,” he added. “We've been very picky about the projects we do and very picky about who we do them with … I've actually talked to our customer since the elections. This project is going to happen.”

Gaudette noted that “prices in ERCOT are depressed,” which is built into the company’s 2027 guidance and long-term outlook, he said.

“Right now we're in a world where battery build and solar have kind of dominated the last two years of build, and demand hasn't been fast enough to absorb all of it,” he added. Gaudette called 2027 “weak,” but noted that the ERCOT region has a strong pipeline overall.

“When you look into the queue in ERCOT, it's not just data centers,” he said. “There's multiple gigawatts of manufacturing facilities, expansions of industrial facilities. Those are coming. Those have jobs. Those are going to hit the grid and sop up some of that excess capacity … NRG is very well positioned to capture value both on the retail side and the generation side as this market tightens and our customers need us more.”

#5756. Trump admin ‘pauses’ leases for five offshore wind projects already under construction

The U.S. Dept. of the Interior has immediately paused the leases for all large-scale offshore wind projects under construction in the United States due to “national security risks identified by the Dept. of War in recently completed classified reports.”

“The prime duty of the United States government is to protect the American people,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “Today’s action addresses emerging national security risks, including the rapid evolution of the relevant adversary technologies, and the vulnerabilities created by large-scale offshore wind projects with proximity near our East Coast population centers. The Trump administration will always prioritize the security of the American people.”

The Dept. of the Interior claims that the blade movement and reflective towers create “radar interference called ‘clutter.'” Allegedly, this is a national security risk.

Dominion Energy released the following statement in response to the pause issued for the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project:

“The Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project (CVOW) is essential for American national security and meeting Virginia’s dramatically growing energy needs, the fastest growth in America. This growth is driven by the need to provide reliable power to many of America’s most important war fighting installations, the world’s largest warship manufacturer, and the largest concentration of data centers on the planet as well as the leading edge of the AI revolution.

Stopping CVOW for any length of time will threaten grid reliability for some of the nation’s most important war fighting, AI and civilian assets. It will also lead to energy inflation and threaten thousands of jobs.

CVOW is American-owned and benefits all of our Virginia customers. Our customers are paying for the project after a careful review of project costs and benefits by Virginia state regulators in 2022. These same state regulators, along with numerous federal agencies, oversee our cyber and physical security program, which is among the strongest in the energy industry.

The project has been more than 10 years in the works, involved close coordination with the military, and is located 27 to 44 miles offshore, so far offshore it does not raise visual impact concerns. The project’s two pilot turbines have been operating for five years without causing any impacts to national security.

CVOW enjoys bipartisan support and is within months of generating a massive 2,600 MW to support the fastest growing part of America’s energy grid. This growth serves the largest concentration of critical infrastructure in the world.

Virginia’s All-American, All-Of-The-Above-Energy Plan requires a range of power generation assets, including natural gas, advanced nuclear, and renewables. Virginia needs every electron we can get as our demand for electricity doubles. These electrons will power the data centers that will win the AI race, support our war fighters, and build the nuclear warships needed to maintain our maritime supremacy. Virginia’s grid needs addition of electrons, not subtraction.

We stand ready to do what is necessary to get these vital electrons flowing as quickly as possible.”

#5755. Tesla Starts Selling Cybercab — $30,000*

Well, it’s a big day in Tesla World. The company has officially launched Cybercab sales. You can now order a Cybercab for the starting price of $30,000 (technically, $29,900). That said, there is an asterisk here — actually, there are two asterisks here. First of all, only people who have been invited to order a Cybercab are able to order one right now — there’s no public ordering page. Secondly, if you do order one, you also need to pay for Full Self Driving — or just “Autonomy” as it’s named on the Tesla webpage. That is listed as $299/month.

So, if you extrapolate $299/month across five years (assuming the price is not going to go up in that time), that’s another $17,940. That would bring your total to $47,840. The $17,940 alone would be more than the cost of the used BMW i3 I recently bought (and for less passenger capacity).

Updates (9:26 am ET, November 14): Two more things: A buyer can buy only one car. (They apparently don’t want people ordering a fleet of Cybercabs to operate as a company at this point for some reason.) Cybercabs can only operate, of course, in geofenced areas where they are allowed to operate.

Is nearly $50,000 over five years for a two-seater a good deal? Well, it’s all about that autonomous driving, isn’t it? If you can sit in the car and watch a movie or sleep or work while being driven, the car is clearly going to be worth more than a normal car. If you can send the Cybercab out for taxi services without riding along, it’s clearly worth more than a normal car you have to drive. But, still, is it worth $50,000 across five years? That is the question, and we should find out soon how many people or companies think that’s a good deal.

One important thing to consider, though, is that the car doesn’t come with a steering wheel or pedals (last we’ve heard). That means that once you have the vehicle, you are at the mercy of Tesla and its monthly Autonomy fee. If Tesla decides to raise the fee to $499/month, you presumably have to pay that much or sell the car (or let is sit parked and out of service).

The estimated delivery time for those ordering a Cybercab today is December of this year. You have to pay a $1,000 non-refundable deposit in order to place an order.

So, yes, it is a big, significant day for Tesla. What that ends up meaning, we’ll see….

#5754. enSights brings AI-powered business management to solar and storage operations

By Marie DeFreitas, Contributor | November 16, 2026

As solar and energy storage portfolios grow in both size and complexity, managing performance is just one part of the equation. Owners and operators must also keep track of power purchase agreements (PPAs), warranties, service contracts, billing, compliance requirements and project-level profitability.

enSights is looking to bring those responsibilities together with the launch of its AI Studio, a new addition to its Energy Business Management (EBM) platform. The company announced the launch Nov. 10.

The AI Studio is designed to give solar and storage owners, operators, and asset managers access to a customizable team of AI specialists that can support business and operational workflows. Through no-code tools, users can create AI dashboards and reports using natural-language instructions, while still establishing their own workflows, routines, data-access permissions and approval requirements.

The approach here reflects a broader shift toward renewable energy software, it’s moving beyond monitoring individual assets toward managing the financial and operational performance of entire portfolios.

According to enSights, its EBM platform brings together energy management systems (EMS), production data, billing, PPA information, operations and maintenance, contractual obligations and compliance on a unified data foundation. That integration is central to the company’s AI strategy.

Rather than limiting AI applications to identifying equipment issues or answering generation-related questions, the platform is designed to connect energy production with the contracts and financial obligations associated with each project.

The AI Studio includes an orchestrator that coordinates specialized AI agents focused on areas like monitoring, operations, revenue, warranties, permits, lenders, insurers, and asset management. For portfolio managers, those capabilities could help reduce the time spent reviewing disconnected systems and manually reconciling information across departments. Automated reviews of contractual obligations, revenue performance and operational alerts could also help teams identify issues earlier and direct attention to matters that still require human intervention.

The enSights AI Studio dashboard provides solar and energy storage operators with AI-powered tools for asset management, operational workflows, and financial oversight. Credit: enSights

enSights emphasized that people remain in control of the AI Team. Users determine which workflows the agents handle and where approvals are required. Physical asset controls remain governed by established EMS and site-level systems.

The AI Studio also builds on an expanded financial management offering within the EBM platform. Its Financial Asset Management Module includes revenue assurance, contract, and obligation management, and profit-and-loss reporting.

The module is intended to provide project-level financial visibility, helping companies identify and prevent revenue losses while generating reports for investors.

The platform also includes real-time EMS, weather and tariff forecasting, along with dispatch planning intended to optimize revenue while maintaining grid safety and local compliance.

enSights says its platform is deployed globally across more than 100,000 sites, representing over 5 GW of assets. The company plans to demonstrate the AI Studio and its broader EBM platform at RE+ 2026.

As AI gains traction across the clean energy industry, the next competitive advantage could come from connecting operational intelligence with the financial and contractual decisions that determine how successfully renewable energy portfolios perform.

#5753. Zoox Expands Robotaxi Service in Las Vegas

Zoox, one of the three leading robotaxi companies in the United States so far, has just expanded commercial robotaxi service in Sin City, the city of Las Vegas. “We are expanding our service beyond the Strip into Downtown and the Arts District, while continuing to add access to even more major resort and entertainment venues across Las Vegas. This follows recent service launches at destinations like Harry Reid International Airport, Sphere, and T-Mobile Arena,” Zoox shares. (Ironic that service has expanded to Harry Reid International Airport just after the huge blue tsunami swept across the United States in the midterm elections.)

Zoox keeps going: “The next evolution of our robotaxi has now made its debut in Las Vegas, introducing the lighter interior and increased comfort to riders. We have also expanded our service hours to be 6:00 a.m.-3:00 a.m., seven days a week, giving riders more opportunity to ride with Zoox.

“The latest information about where riders can travel to/from can be found in the Zoox app.”

The company also notes that it launched limited robotaxi service in Las Vegas a little more than a year ago. While it’s still not close to huge, it has expanded greatly since launch and continues to display incremental progress. “On September 10, 2025, we officially launched the Zoox service on and around the Las Vegas Strip. Rides are available through the Zoox app, which can be downloaded on both iOS and Android devices. This moment marked Zoox as the first company in history to provide a fully autonomous ride-hailing service in a purpose-built robotaxi,” the company adds.

Here’s more info on how to ride with Zoox in Las Vegas: “After downloading the Zoox app, riders can choose from a range of destinations on the Strip, into Downtown, and the Arts District. “At Harry Reid International Airport, our locations are conveniently situated near the Terminal 1 departures and baggage claim at both Terminal 1 and 3. For all other destinations, Zoox picks up and drops off riders in the designated rideshare areas.

“To help riders identify their robotaxi, riders can use FindMyZoox, a feature in the app where the robotaxi uses distinct lighting and sound cues to help riders identify their specific robotaxi in crowded pickup zones. The app will also include the vehicle’s license plate number, estimated pickup times, real-time arrival updates, and post-ride summaries with feedback options. If riders need support before, during, or after their ride, they can contact a member of our remote Zoox support team through the app or via the “Help” button located on the rider screen within the robotaxi.”

One thing that stands out with Zoox is that it uses a purpose-built vehicle rather than adapting a normal consumer car for robotaxi use. Also, that vehicle is quite a bit different from what we see from others. “Our purpose-built robotaxi creates a fundamentally different cabin experience: carriage-style seating where four passengers face each other, minimal screen distraction, and space to unwind or connect. Whether you’re catching up with friends after a show, celebrating a night out, or just taking in the city, the journey itself becomes part of the experience. That’s what riders in Las Vegas are choosing when they ride Zoox.”

2026 has been a year of significant robotaxi news. One might say it’s been the year of the robotaxi. “The autonomous vehicle industry has made remarkable strides this year, bringing us closer to a future of safer, more accessible mobility. With the launch of our fully driverless ride-hailing service using a purposefully designed robotaxi, we’re thrilled to be part of this groundbreaking journey,” adds Aicha Evans, CEO of Zoox. “Las Vegas is a city famous for unforgettable moments, and it is the ideal location for our debut. Zoox is about transforming the entire ride-hailing experience, making every ride a delightful experience.”

#5752. The Best Rental Car Companies In 2026 According To JD Power

Many auto dealerships have a well-earned reputation for making life difficult for customers, but it doesn't always get easier trying to rent. Whether they're charging customers for breaking the laws of physics or relying on AI scanners to bill $440 for a wheel scuff, rental car agencies obviously have some work to do when it comes to boosting customer satisfaction. The good news is that that seems to be happening.

According to the JD Power 2026 North America Rental Car Satisfaction Study, overall customer satisfaction saw some notable improvements over 2025 — especially in two key areas. First, 90% of rental car customers said that, when they arrived at the counter, a vehicle from the class they reserved was waiting for them. That is, they reserved a mid-size sedan and one was there. Getting a bit more detailed, 85% claimed they "were able to pick a specific vehicle within the class they were given." Those figures were up 3 and 5 percentage points, respectively. Meanwhile, the study's average satisfaction score went from 691 in 2025 — on a 1,000-point scale — to 707 this year.

As for what goes into the results, JD Power bases them on ease of rental, pick-up/drop-off, level of trust, vehicle, staff, value for price paid, and digital tools. Those seven "core dimensions" are then weighted in the order they're listed. The outcome for 2026 was that six of 13 agencies finished with above-average scores, led by Enterprise, National, Advantage Rent A Car, Alamo, Sixt, and Hertz. Bringing up the rear were Thrifty and Dollar. Finally, all this data comes from 7,845 survey respondents, all of whom had rented their cars from airport-based rental companies in the span between August 2025 and August 2026.

It's worth pointing out that all 13 rental agencies earned higher study scores this year than last, with a lot of that improvement coming at the lower levels. Dollar, for instance, was at the very bottom of the rankings for both 2025 and 2026, yet its score jumped from 641 to 663. The biggest advance in terms of points was for Payless — it went from 11th place with 650 points last year to 8th place with 699 points this time around.

The standings didn't change much at the other end of the spectrum, though. The order remained the same, with Enterprise setting the pace, followed by National and Advantage Rent A Car, and they each saw essentially the same improvements: Enterprise was up 5 points to 739, National improved the same amount to 726 points, and Advantage advanced 6 points, rising from 711 to 717. (Technically, Advantage was tied with Sixt in 2025. Despite a three-point bump in its satisfaction score, that last agency slipped to fifth place in 2026, falling behind Alamo's 716 points.)

Oh, and there's one other factoid you should keep in mind about the rental car agencies: every major rental car brand in the country is owned by one of three companies.

Enterprise Mobility owns Enterprise, of course, but it has National and Alamo under its umbrella as well. Likewise, Avis Budget Group controls its namesake rental brands plus Payless, and Hertz has its own trio that extends to Dollar and Thrifty. Hertz also had purchased Advantage and owned that brand for a time. It's just that when Hertz bought Dollar and Thrifty in 2012, the FTC forced Hertz to sell off Advantage to maintain a competitive market.

#5751. The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine.

On November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms. It is an impressive area and a modest opening price for a prospective new metals industry. The difference between the two numbers helps explain what the sale is actually offering.

The winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions. The government has said explicitly that an issued lease does not authorize commercial harvesting. It allows preliminary work such as mapping, while physical exploration, testing and mining require additional plans and approvals. The lease does not establish reserves, a collector that can work for years, a processing plant or buyers willing to pay enough for the metals.

The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone. Investors should pay close attention to the difference between a government auction and an operating mining project. A mineral lease can have speculative value long before a profitable business exists.

In my new TFIE Strategy Briefing on the American Samoa auction, I examine how federal leasing can advance while the integrated business case remains weak.

The acreage has no direct relationship to the amount of commercially recoverable metal. The final federal notice describes northern and southern areas of roughly 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres. They are regulatory boundaries. A mining company needs deposit-grade and abundance data, continuity, recoverable tonnage, processing recoveries and a market price that leaves a margin after all the offshore and downstream costs.

The geology is becoming better understood. In April 2026, US Geological Survey scientists deployed 38 box cores in the Samoa Basin, of which 36 yielded enough material for nodule-density measurements. The expedition report is useful new evidence about the region. It is an expedition summary rather than a reserve statement for either lease area. Mineral distributions vary within the sampled region, and the better-studied Clarion-Clipperton Zone is not an adequate substitute for American Samoa’s own geological evidence.

Collection creates another set of costs. Impossible Metals proposes autonomous vehicles that select nodules and return to a support vessel. The Metals Company uses a more mature crawler-and-riser approach that has demonstrated recovery at pilot scale. Both must turn offshore demonstrations into dependable annual production, with maintenance, ship time, recovery systems and delays included. Their technologies should not be assigned the same engineering maturity, but neither has proved a profitable integrated mining-and-processing business.

In 2025, metallurgical engineer Lyle Trytten and I completed an independent techno-economic assessment commissioned by the National Ocean Protection Coalition. We examined both collection approaches, offshore operations, processing, metal markets and financial sensitivities. We judged commercial viability within the following 15 years highly unlikely. A new leasing process has not supplied the operating and financial evidence that was missing in that assessment.

The history of first-of-a-kind offshore production should influence the financing. Nautilus Minerals spent substantial capital on its Solwara-1 venture without reaching commercial production. Deep-sea mining depends on specialized machines, ships, handling systems, processing capacity and sales contracts working in sequence. The first production years of comparable projects are rarely smooth. The lease is one of the cheapest and earliest commitments in that chain.

American Samoa also has its own decision to make. Its government has supported scientific investigation while withholding support for commercial extraction at present. A lawsuit filed by Samoan chiefs and community groups contests the federal process. The resulting legal and territorial questions matter alongside engineering and economics. The environmental finding for preliminary leasing activities is not a finding about the effects of a future commercial mine.

Auction results will show what qualified bidders will pay for an opportunity. A winning bid can justify a company’s further studies and improve its fundraising story. An operating business will require years of capital investment, production evidence and profitable metal sales. Those are much harder milestones, and they remain ahead of the bidders.

Read A Seabed Lease Does Not Fix a Broken Business Case for the full assessment of the auction, and the Barnard–Trytten report for the underlying engineering and financial analysis.

#5750. 'If They Can Get In Here, It Is What It Is' Detroit Bus Driver Welcomes Two Horses To Board

There's no arguing that the people of the city of Detroit tend to keep things interesting. Earlier this year, a priest punched the fear of God into a fleeing teen driver after a crash. The latest stunt to capture the nation's attention was two young Detroit men taking their horses onto a city bus. The outing was Raven's first time in the big city, according to the Detroit Free Press. Raven is one of 12 horses Jordan Williams uses as part of his Urban City Cowboys program: a Western rodeo school outside of Detroit, as well as an organization that offers equestrian therapy to children with disabilities.

Williams was one of the two men involved in the horse-meets-bus adventure. The other was a close friend who had come along with his horse for a fundraiser earlier in the day. While riding near 7 Mile Road, they had stopped near a Detroit Department of Transportation bus stop. One of the buses had also stopped for them and the driver asked if they wanted on. If you listen to the video circulating the internet compiled from the cameras on the DDOT bus, you can hear the driver say to Williams and his friend, "If they can get in here, it is what it is."

At one point you hear the amused bus driver mention something about the horses being service animals, and Williams responding with a joking "yup." The driver then lowered a ramp that would allow the horses to more easily walk aboard. Sure enough, both Raven and the other horse entered the bus with the men, trotted down the aisle, and exited from the rear side exit as the automated greeting told the horses, "Welcome aboard." The horses never stayed on the bus, though. They really did a quick walk through.

This wasn't the first time one of Williams' horses has boarded a Detroit-area bus. He told WXYZ 7 that he intended for the stunt to make a splash, as he's had horses "on Jefferson, we've been on the Chalmers, we've been on the Connors and now on the 7 Mile." This was Raven's first bus adventure, though. Raven is a 12-year-old horse, and one of Williams' newest. Along with his 11 other horses, he watches 10 horses for individuals on his 10-acre property in Romulus, along with the typical barnyard set up of chickens, goats, pigs, a cow, barn cats, dogs, a parrot, snake, and others.

DDOT issued a statement to WXYZ November 10 that said it is "taking the appropriate steps to address this incident as it is not consistent with DDOT policy and potentially creates an unsafe and uncomfortable ride for our passengers." The rider in the video seemed to be the only person on the bus at the time, and appeared pretty chill about the whole experience while he took some pictures. Also, it could be argued that the horses didn't technically "ride" the bus. It never moved while they were on board.

The city is using the recent attention as a way to train everyone at DDOT to "make sure they're aware of different policies," i.e. service animals. A statement from the city said that they recognized "that the actions in the video were meant to draw awareness to a positive cause. The City of Detroit also stands ready to assist our local entrepreneurs by connecting them with programs and opportunities that safely increase awareness of their organizations, and helps them expand their positive impact on our City."

Williams' act was truly wholesome, and of course people understand horses don't technically belong on a bus, or in a city environment with all those dangerous cars. Take it from last city to truly hold out on keeping horses around — New York City, which finally voted away its famous horse carriages in October.

#5749. The Chevy El Camino Launched In 1959, And This Is The Ute's Most Sought-After Model Year

No, the Chevy El Camino wasn't the first to combine a two-door car with an open bed truck. The first production vehicle to do that was a Ford, but possibly not the one you're thinking of. A design engineer named Lew Bandt, then with Ford of Australia, developed what's often considered the original factory-made ute — the 1934 Ford Model 40-A Light Delivery. Depending on exactly how you define a ute, some folks point to the 1927 Volvo OV4 as well.

Of course, it was the 1957 Ford Ranchero that truly inspired the El Camino. The Ranchero was built on the Blue Oval's full-size platform of the time, and it became both relatively popular and relatively profitable for the automaker. In fact, it was successful enough that Chevy was inspired to get in on the ute action with its full-size 1959 El Camino. Originally a short-lived model only in production for that year and 1960, the El Camino would get a second chance at life in 1964. That's when the Bowtie brand revived the name and brought it back in slightly downsized form on the same platform as the intermediate-class Chevrolet Chevelle.

This is where things start to get interesting for gearheads. In 1970, Chevrolet introduced a 454-cubic-inch LS6 V8 that was reserved for both the Chevelle and its platform mate. With that mill standing out as the most powerful unit of the year, the former became a muscle-car legend and one of Dom Toretto's rides in the epic 10-movie "Fast and Furious" saga. Meanwhile, the latter turned into perhaps the most sought-after El Camino of them all, the 1970 El Camino SS LS6 454. Keep in mind that this was a whole different engine than the LS6 in the 200-mph 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray.

There are two key reasons that enthusiasts crave this machine. Right off the bat, the 1970 El Camino SS 454 was a one-year wonder — its exact powerplant was the aggressive LS6 V8 that would be dropped from the El Camino for 1971. True, Chevy sold a 1971 El Camino SS 454, but that mill was the less-powerful LS5. As far as actual production numbers for the 1970 model, those are hard to come by. Hemmings says 4,475 Chevrolets in total were sold with the LS6 for that year, but they were spread out among both Chevelles and El Caminos.

The second major selling point here is the outrageous driving experience offered by these rides, and for that, credit also goes to their incredible engine. Factory rated at 450 horsepower with a whopping 500 pound-feet of torque, this motor featured a cast-iron block and heads along with an 11.25:1 compression ratio. Also adding to the muscle are a four-bolt main block, a four-barrel Holley carburetor, and a high-performance camshaft. The outcome was that both the El Camino and Chevelle could serve up more horses than not just the 1970 Corvette, but all other production cars, too.

As further proof of just how hard people are jonesing for the 1970 El Camino SS LS6 454, an example may hold the record for the highest auction price for any El Camino — the car went for $275,000 at a Barrett-Jackson sale in 2023. Just remember auction values can change quickly: one 1970 Chevelle LS6 lost its owner a million dollars.

#5748. Zoox Launches Robotaxis in Atlanta

The year of the robotaxi rolls on. Just after writing about Zoox expanding its robotaxi service in Las Vegas, I see news that Zoox is entering Atlanta!

“Our initial rollout will focus on the Northwest region of Atlanta, near Atlantic Station, Woodward, and Home Park. We will expand throughout the year as our testing progresses,” Zoox shares.

To start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. But that should change fairly soon. “We look forward to opening our waitlist for Atlanta in the coming months, ahead of the launch of our Zoox Explorers early rider program.”

I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Or is it companies rushing to try to prove their viability and build up economies of scale, but which might not actually be financially viable and profitable in the long run — or even next year? We’ll have to wait to see. In the meantime, it’s certainly exciting each time a new area is opened up and more electric robotaxis hit the road.

In case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the company informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. This is in addition to testing in Austin and Miami, our public service in Las Vegas, and our Zoox Explorers early rider program in San Francisco.”

Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. It has been laying the groundwork for this launch for about a year and a half in the city. “We started operations in Atlanta in the Spring of 2025, using our testing fleet to map and learn about local driving behaviors, weather patterns, and the city infrastructure. Since then, we have been steadily expanding our driving capabilities, including beginning autonomous driving, and growing our geofence, fleet size, and team to prepare for this next stage of testing.” Zoox explains further how this is central to how Zoox operates:

“Zoox has always been thoughtful and measured in our approach to rolling out autonomous technology at every level. Before we even hit the road and begin driving with our testing fleet in any capacity, we first engage with local and state officials and regulators. Our philosophy is ‘no surprises’ as we lay the foundations for future service markets.

“Along with engaging with local and state officials and regulators, we also love partnering with the community. Workforce development starts long before a first job. That’s why we’re partnering with @Promise Center to help local youth learn, grow, and prepare for their futures in a safe, supportive environment. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”

Circling back to Atlanta and why the company has made that one of the first cities for its robotaxi deployment, Zoox adds the following: “Atlanta is a dynamic, vibrant city. Known as the ‘Silicon Valley of the South,’ it boasts one of the largest ride-hailing markets in the United States. Atlanta’s dense, urban layout creates strong demand for efficient transportation solutions, which is where on-demand autonomous ride-hailing comes in. It also has a growing population, and demand like this is exactly why we’re excited to bring Zoox to Atlantans.”

Lastly, as I also highlighted in my article last night about Zoox expanding in Las Vegas, one key thing Zoox is proud of and argues sets it apart from the competition is how vertically integrated its robotaxi business is and how useful the design of its vehicle is for its purpose. Here’s more: “While Atlanta has become a hub for autonomous testing, Zoox continues to stand apart from other companies. Unlike the retrofitted solutions currently on the road, our robotaxi was built from the ground up for fully autonomous ride-hailing. It has no steering wheel or driver’s seat, instead featuring spacious, carriage-style seating for up to four passengers. This design layout allows us to offer Zoox passengers more than just a ride; we are providing a private space where riders can socialize, relax, and reclaim their time. […]

“Zoox owns, operates, and assembles its vehicles, and is the only company currently deploying a fully driverless, purpose-built robotaxi on public roads in the U.S.

“We see promise in bringing our robotaxi service to Atlanta, and look forward to offering Atlantans this unique and private space to socialize, rock out, and create their own experience while being transported to their destination.”

You can learn more on the Zoox website or the Zoox app.

#5747. This 40-Year-Old Econobox Has The Top EPA MPG Rating Of Any Non-Hybrid Production Car

Welp, we may have finally reached a turning point. Yes, short-sighted automakers have been supporting Trump's move to roll back fuel-economy standards. But voters seemed to have had other ideas on Election Day 2026, when the Dems secured both the Senate and House. Of course, while that may stop some of the madness, we're unlikely to see another fuel-sipper like the 1986 Chevrolet Sprint ER anytime soon. Chevy's tiny captive import originally posted an EPA highway rating of 60 mpg, a mark that no other non-electrified production car in the country has matched since. Plus, that highway score was complemented by ratings of 55 mpg in the city and 57 mpg combined.

Now, we'll get into some of the details about the Sprint ER below, but first let's head off some possible objections at the pass. The most important is that the EPA made a major change in how it calculates fuel efficiency back in 2007 and then retroactively updated its database. As a result, the 1986 Sprint ER currently shows an EPA line of 44 mpg city/53 mpg highway/48 mpg combined. That makes for decreases of approximately 20%/12%/16% compared to its original fuel-economy grades.

Some drivers have also topped 60 mpg in real-world diesel driving. A writer for Car and Driver, for example, hypermiled a 2017 Chevy Cruze diesel to the tune of 70 mpg over a test run of about 160 miles. It's just that diesel engines have some drawbacks of their own.

In a way, the genesis of the Chevy Sprint goes back to some of America's earlier meddling in the Middle East. The CIA had put Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in control of Iran in 1953 — forcing out that country's democratically elected prime minister — and the shah was then overthrown himself as part of the 1979 Iranian Revolution. That led to the oil crisis of the same year, which helped convince GM to enter a three-way partnership with Isuzu and Suzuki in 1981. The goal was to build high-efficiency cars that were, basically, too small for GM to build at the time.

One of those cars was the JDM Suzuki Cultus, a car that would be renamed the Swift in Europe in 1985 and be rebadged as the Chevrolet Sprint for the same year. It also served as the Pontiac Firefly, but only in Canada. Now, this wasn't as tiny as a kei car, but it certainly wasn't big. That 1986 Sprint checked in at 144 inches long, 60 inches wide, and 53 inches tall — so it was about 1 inch longer than the 2022 Chevy Spark, but also 2.8 inches narrower, 5.4 inches shorter in height, and 774 pounds lighter. After all, the Sprint ER, a three-door hatchback, tipped the scales at only 1,504 pounds.

Yet svelte dimensions weren't the only factors in play. The regular Sprint was motivated by a 1.0-liter I3 engine capable of 48 horsepower, and Suzuki had revised the camshaft for the ER version. It made a significant difference, since the non-ER model had an original EPA line of 44/50/47 (37/45/40 in today's ratings).

For this section, please keep in mind we're going to level the playing field by using the post-2008 EPA ratings for the Sprint ER — which, as a reminder, features a fuel-economy line of 44/53/48 with its standard five-speed manual gearbox. Nowadays, the most fuel-efficient non-electrified car in the country is the 2026 Honda Civic that can see 32/41/36 with its 2.0-liter I4 motor and CVT. The 2026 Civic Hybrid, as an FYI, can raise the efficiency bar to 50/47/49.

The latter model isn't the country's most efficient hybrid, either. For that, we have to turn to the Toyota Prius.
