#5746. Study Pinpoints States with Steepest Warming Trends Since 1980

The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, currently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius. While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being.

To that end, a new open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets (MERRA2 and ERA5) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state.

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C.

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” says MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser, a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

By Mark Dwortzan | Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, MIT

#5745. High Speed Rail Isn't Just Fast Trains, There Are Rigidly Defined Categories

The uninformed often fall for the illusion that high-speed rail is simply a railroad operating extremely fast trains. In actuality, it's an entire transportation system tightly regulated by government agencies. The Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) attempted to spur high-speed rail development in 2018 by letting operators run high-speed trains on existing speed-limited infrastructure, but so far, no new service has usurped Amtrak's Acela on the Northeast Corridor as America's fastest train. Businesses simply won't buy passenger trains capable of hitting 220 miles per hour if they don't have the dedicated right-of-way needed to reach top speed.

The FRA defines three tiers of Passenger Equipment Safety Standards delineated by top speed. Each increasing tier requires more stringent crashworthiness, maintenance, and safety standards. Most passenger trains in the United States fall under Tier I, which is limited to 125 mph. Tier II, or higher-speed rail, has a legal top speed of 160 mph. Tier III, established in 2018, allows for speeds up to 220 mph. However, the trains are only half of the equation.

The agency stipulates that high-speed trains can't travel faster than 160 mph on any track with at-grade crossings. Even tracks with a 160 mph limit are rare in the U.S., as the Northeast Corridor has only four short stretches where Acela trains are allowed to touch 160 mph. The rest of the route between Boston and Washington, D.C. is limited to 125 mph. With as many as 386 passengers on board, there can't be any risk of anyone or anything entering the tracks and causing a catastrophic crash.

Japan's Shinkansen is viewed as the archetypal form of high-speed rail. The moniker translates into English as "new main line." Japanese National Railways opened the first Shinkansen line between Tokyo and Osaka in 1964. The five-year construction effort created a new dedicated high-speed main line, separate from commuter and freight traffic on the parallel Tōkaidō Main Line. France's TGV and other high-speed networks in Europe borrowed this dedicated-infrastructure philosophy from the Shinkansen.

Florida's Brightline is the most prominent U.S. example of the failings of shared rights-of-way. The higher-speed service between Miami and Orlando is heavily constrained by its 325-mile route, specifically the portion shared with the Florida East Coast Railway. According to Brightline, its trains are limited to 79 mph along this section. The 67-mile stretch between Miami and West Palm Beach, owned by the freight service, has 156 at-grade crossings. The abundance of crossings creates opportunities for trains to hit vehicles and pedestrians. Brightline-involved collisions have killed over 200 people since 2017. Dedicated rights-of-way are not only faster, they are far safer.

#5744. AI Businesses Still Bleeding Billions

AI is fun and cool when it creates useful things for you or answers tough questions quickly and well (let’s not focus on AI slop and false claims at the moment), but that doesn’t mean AI businesses are financially sustainable or sensible. AI companies are still heavily subsidizing their broad use, with the benefits for them being growing user bases and sky-high valuations. These companies are burning billions of dollars each quarter on the hype and promise that they will rule the world one day (quite literally).

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

One might think that means not a lot changed, and certainly nothing positive. However, the company’s revenue was actually up by 50%! So, even with a huge boost in revenue, gigantic losses grew! Furthermore, the company was apparently even using a tool of “last resort” here.

OpenAI started running ads in ChatGPT, something that the company was adamantly trying to avoid. CEO Sam Altman previously called the proposal to run ads “unsettling” and claimed that the company would only go that route as a matter of “last resort.” Well, it seems the company has reached that point of last resort. And that can’t be a good thing, right? Considering that OpenAI is still losing billions of dollars a quarter, it’s even more concerning. What comes after a “last resort” effort to turn finances around?

Frankly, I wish we could spend billions of dollars a quarter to make CleanTechnica into a behemoth of a media organization! That would be amazing — imagine all of the stuff we could do! But what are the chances we’d be losing billions of dollars a quarter in doing so? And how long could we operate like that before external sources of funding stopped covering the bill?

As we know, OpenAI is one of the “leaders” of the AI industry. If it is struggling like this, who isn’t, and what does that mean for the industry overall and where it’s headed?

The one big player that has been raking in the dough in the midst of this enormous AI craze is NVIDIA, and look at what’s now happening there! Where are things going to go with that company?

“The news comes not long after controversy over how OpenAI was projecting its earnings. In October, the company reported an annualized revenue, an estimate of how much money it will earn over a year, of about $50 billion — which was $20 billion short of what it told investors only a month before,” Futurism adds. “The discrepancy was taken as an admission that the business models of AI companies weren’t as robust as their leadership was making them out to be, fueling speculation of an impending bubble.”

Why can’t the leaders of these companies just ask their chatbots how to turn a profit and implement their answers? Well, one of the answers might have been regulatory capture and blocking others from entering the market, but that dream may now be out the window. In my humble opinion, 2027 could be a very interesting year for AI companies, and that might involve a big popping noise.

#5743. Two-Seat SUVs Are Stupendously Rare

The Suzuki X-90 seems to be the only two-seat SUV made for the mass market on a global scale. With that as our influence, we went in search of other two-seat SUVs to find out if they are as stupendously rare as the first appeared. After all, by their very definition, SUVs are supposed to be utilitarian vehicles, and there is nothing practical about a two-seat layout.

If the search were for two-door SUVs, the list might be a little longer and would include the Jeep Wrangler – including the Scrambler SRT Concept. However, even these usually have a rear row of seats, so they do not qualify as a two-seat SUV. And most single-cab pickup trucks are also disqualified, even if an argument can be made that they are SUVs – of a type.

So back to that little Suzuki of the 1990s. Single-handedly trying to launch a whole new segment of two-seat SUVs, and clearly failing, the X-90 might not seem like it qualifies as a full-blown SUV. After all, it was only 146 inches long and had a 95-horsepower 1.6-liter engine, which are not the normal stats that define an SUV.

But the X-90 did use traditional body-on-frame construction, like proper 4x4s, and also came with four-wheel drive and a live rear axle. Diminutive Suzuki off-roaders have an enviable reputation in the automotive world for going further into the wilderness than their stature suggests, so do not discount the X-90's trail abilities.

The X-90 was not a hit, though. Its biggest market in the world was the U.S., where only 7,205 found homes in a three-year period from 1996 onwards. So, after the weirdness of the small Suzuki, are there any other vehicles like it out there? Any other two-seat SUVs at all?

Swiss firm Sbarro is known for creating motoring oddities. Among its back catalog are a VW Golf-sized hatchback powered by a Ferrari V8 (though not the one Ducati once built for a Lancia sedan) and an open-topped version of the Renault Espace minivan. But Sbarro also gave us one of the rare two-seat SUVs in the world, in the shape of the Monster G of 1987. This had a spec like no other SUV in history, mainly because the wheels were taken directly from a Boeing 727 airliner.

Other details included an adapted chassis from a Range Rover, a Mercedes 6.3-liter V8 under the hood delivering 350 horsepower, and a folding motorcycle and a portable generator mounted in the trunk of the Monster G. This Sbarro was built as a one-off commission for a wealthy German enthusiast, so you'd be forgiven for not having heard of it.

In a similar vein, French firm Aixam gave the world another unusual two-seat SUV, in the form of the Mega Track. As a lifted V12-powered supercar – using the engine from the W140 Mercedes S-Class – the Mega Track is more of a precursor to the likes of the Lamborghini Huracan Sterrato and Porsche 911 Dakar than it is a traditional SUV.

The Mega Track was huge, measuring 196.85 inches long and 98.4 inches wide, while also weighing more than 4,400 lb, and it joins the list of rare two-seat SUVs. It also had four-wheel drive and the ability to increase its ground clearance at the press of a button. In comparison to the Sbarro, this car was commonplace, with about five or six vehicles created, but yeah, it's a rare example of a rare genre by any measure.

Following on from the Willys Jeep's use in World War II, it was a logical next step to turn it into a civilian vehicle. Initially, CJ-1 and CJ-2 derivatives were designed primarily as agricultural vehicles that could be used in fields, and by 1945 the CJ-2A was born. This was produced until 1949, and more than 214,000 units were made.

In its most basic form, the CJ-2A wouldn't qualify as a two-seat SUV, as it came with just a driver's seat, although options included a passenger seat and/or a rear bench, so we're adding it to the list. It was possible to remove the rear bench in the original Willys Jeep, of course, turning it into a two-seater. Does anyone consider the Willys Jeep an SUV, though? Probably not.

And while an 80-year-old Jeep may still have the goods, there's a breed of new commercial SUVs in markets across the world which could also qualify as two-seaters, though not many are offered to North American buyers. One example is Toyota's long-serving Land Cruiser, which can trace its origins back to 1951. The current model is sold as a commercial vehicle, and while it looks like the standard civilian station wagon, it in fact has just two seats up front and a mesh ahead of the load area.

Similarly, in some international markets, the current Defender 90 is sold as a commercial vehicle known as the Hard Top, which has just two seats up front. Saying that, Land Rover Classic will restore and "remaster" an old Defender, fitting a 405-horsepower V8 in the process. Among the body styles offered is the "90 Hard Top", which has a two-seat cabin. That, and the "90" part of its name, are about all the Defender shares with the Suzuki X-90.

#5742. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

#5741. Fabric Molds Could Bring Material-Saving Concrete Beams Within Reach

MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.

Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.

Now, MIT engineers have shown that highly efficient beams can be cast in something more accessible: sewn fabric. In a paper published in the Journal of Building Engineering, the team designed and built a 3-meter (about 10-foot) test beam using fabric molds created through an automated pattern-making process. Compared with a conventional beam designed to carry the same weight, the optimized beam used about one-third as much concrete and half as much steel reinforcement. When tested, its measured response was within about 2 percent of what the team’s computer model predicted.

Fabric formwork, in which concrete is poured into a mold made of textile, has been explored for years to create beams that vary in depth, rather than in rectangular shapes common in construction. But because fabric deforms under the weight of wet concrete, that flexibility has made the final shape hard to predict.

“The key realization was that this flexibility is not just a limitation to manage; with the right computational pattern design, it can become a way to produce optimized structural forms,” says Josephine Carstensen, the Gilbert W. Winslow (1937) Career Development Professor in Civil Engineering and senior author of the study.

Fabric molds can also be inexpensive, lightweight, and fast compared to wood or steel molds. “You could sew a formwork together off site, pack it into a box, and bring it to a job site very easily,” says Jackson Jewett PhD ’25, co-author of the study. “We joke that we are developing the H&M of the construction industry.”

Cement production accounts for roughly 8 percent of human-caused carbon emissions.

“This work addresses concrete’s climate footprint primarily by reducing material demand,” Carstensen says. “Cement production is highly carbon-intensive, so using less concrete is an important part of decarbonizing construction.”

Where new construction happens matters, too. The world’s number of buildings is expected to nearly double by 2050, with about 85 percent of that growth in developing countries, where access to advanced construction equipment is often limited. That is why, Carstensen says, the team focused on an accessible, cost-conscious fabrication approach.

Concrete is strong when compressed, but weak when pulled, so it’s reinforced with steel that can handle the pulling forces. The researchers first mapped a path for the steel reinforcement using a method called graphic statics, which can generate structural designs almost instantly. They used it to shape the steel bar so that it carries an equal share of the weight along its entire length to keep the reinforcement simple enough for builders to make. Topology optimization, which works more slowly but can place material freely, was used to determine where concrete was needed and where material could be removed from areas where it contributes little to the structural performance.

“Both methods are good at different things, so we tried to combine the strengths of both into a single methodology,” says Jewett.

The resulting beam has a top section, narrow angled legs, and a thin bottom section for the steel reinforcement. The team’s automated process translated the 3D beam design into flat fabric pieces that can be cut and sewn into a mold, accounting for how the fabric will deform once concrete is poured in. A simple timber frame supported the finished fabric mold.

For Mark Hellrich SM ’26, the study’s lead author, the main hands-on challenge was getting the concrete mix right. Woven cotton fabric lets water seep through, so a mix that is too runny loses water through the mold. It also presses harder against the fabric, pushing it away from the intended shape.

The team used a moderately wet, sand-rich mix with only small stones, so the concrete could flow through the beam’s narrow, angled legs and thin bottom section without getting stuck. They then packed it in by hand, prodding each layer and tapping and kneading the fabric from the outside.

“This is where the flexibility of the mold becomes an advantage: you can work the concrete through the interconnected passages without a vibrator, which a rigid mold of this shape would need,” says Hellrich. A concrete vibrator is a tool typically used to shake air pockets out of freshly poured concrete in rigid molds.

Once the concrete was in place, the wet fabric revealed the beam’s final shape. “All three beams were free of wrinkles and creases,” says Hellrich. The top surface stayed close to the design, while the main difference was a downward sag along the bottom, with the angled legs folding slightly inward.

To find out how much sewing precision the beam needs, the team built three molds for the same design, made from 36, 56, and 76 fabric pieces. Comparing the 3D scans of the cast beams with the target design, the researchers found that more seams gave finer control over the details, but did not necessarily make the beam’s overall shape more accurate.

“More seams improve local control because they divide the fabric into smaller, more constrained panels. But a more complex pattern also has more pieces to align and more seam length, so small cutting, sewing, and assembly inaccuracies can accumulate across the mold, explains Carstensen.

The 56-piece mold demonstrated the best balance, capturing the important design geometry without the added time, effort, and potential errors associated with the most complex pattern.

The researchers then load-tested one of the beams, gradually stacking 36 water-filled buckets on top of it, up to about 30 percent of its design load to reflect everyday service conditions. Weighted lines hung from the beam’s underside to precise measuring gauges below, tracking how far the beam bent as the load was added and removed. At the beam’s center, the measured deflection — its downward movement under the load — was within about 2 percent of the computer model’s prediction.

The team also compared the cost of a single fabric-formed beam with a conventional one and found that location makes all the difference. In the Global South, where materials tend to cost more relative to labor, all three fabric versions were cheaper, with savings of about 10 to 20 percent. In the Global North, higher labor costs for sewing reversed that advantage, making the fabric versions about 16 to 55 percent more expensive.

The findings suggest that fabric formwork is most promising for custom-shaped concrete components produced as a one-off or in small batches, such as exposed beams, roof or long-span framing, pedestrian structures, and landscape elements. For the repetitive, rectangular beams found in most buildings, conventional reusable molds remain the more economical choice where labor is expensive.

“To get started, a builder would need the digital pattern for the target component, a sewing machine and suitable fabric, and a simple timber support frame,” Carstensen says. “That is a much lower equipment threshold than robotic fabrication, concrete 3D printing, or CNC-milled molds.”

The researchers describe the 3-meter beam as a proof of concept comparable to a short building span. It is also a big step up from the 1.2-meter beam the team built in a previous project, Jewett notes.

Building bigger isn’t just a matter of enlarging the design, Carstensen notes. As a beam gets longer, its own weight and the pressure on the fabric mold change, so a larger beam would need a new design. The next step, Carstensen says, is “to test multiple beams to failure.”

“The nice thing about these optimization methods is they generate structures that look organic,” Jewett says. “Their geometries are clear expressions of how the forces move through the structural system. There is elegance to them. It makes you ask why we don’t design all our structures in this way.”

Joining Carstensen, Jewett, and Hellrich on the paper are co-authors Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, and Emily Whiting, of Boston University’s Department of Computer Science.

The work was partially supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

By Stephanie Martinovich | Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, MIT

#5739. How F1 Transmissions Can Select Two Gears At Once And Keep Racing For 3,000 Miles

There's a bit of madness required to craft F1 cars, let alone drive them. The transmissions have to be able to absorb 3,800 shifts per race, and ideally last at least half the season — because they cost roughly $330,000. However, they're now so reliable, despite enduring tremendous forces, that a prior regulation that restricted each team to five transmissions a season was dropped. Ferrari has said its gearbox can survive for over 3,000 miles without any issues. That's thousands and thousands of gear changes, and just about a whole Formula 1 season.

And an F1 shift happens in as little as 2 milliseconds, versus the leisurely 100 milliseconds it takes a dual-clutch transmission to shift in a supercar. That's a tenth of a second for the street sports car versus a 500th of a second for the F1 car, or 50 times faster per shift. Your mind should melt at that figure — and so, you'd think, would an F1 gearbox.

The reason it doesn't is that the gearbox can transfer load so rapidly that it's nearly in two gears simultaneously — but not exactly. The key here is mechanical. A device called a dog ring handles gear swaps. Through a simple revision of the shape of the ring's teeth, engineers were able to make the dog rings do two jobs at once — grab a gear when one side of its teeth are pushed against it, and if the driver selects another gear, the change in rpm forces the first ring to disengage. The fact that the change happens so quickly is necessary both to prevent double-gear engagement. Simultaneously, this gives teams a critical advantage that's become the motivating force behind F1's transmission arms race.

There were multiple reasons to ditch the manual gearbox in F1. First, if you're toggling a stick-shift gearbox you have to manipulate a clutch with your left foot, which makes it tougher to brake simultaneously. And it means you have to take one hand off the wheel to perform the gear change.

But Ferrari wasn't concerned about the added stress on its drivers when it pioneered paddle-shifting in 1989. Instead, it was chasing aerodynamic efficiency, and the mechanical linkages at the front of the brand's F1 car made it bulkier than if you could eliminate these elements. Which is what Ferrari did, switching to a hydraulic system controlled electronically each time the driver flipped a paddle. While the transmission was a reliability nightmare during its debut season, by 1990 Ferrari was winning with it.

That led to a development war, and by 1993 Williams engineered an even more advanced Continuously Variable Transmission, or CVT, which was banned before it could even compete. Yes, we know your CVT hate is way overblown and bordering on irrational. But Williams' CVT wasn't the widget you're envisioning. Instead, it was the precursor to today's ultra-reliable gearbox, and it could keep an F1 car's engine on the boil, never dropping rpm — exactly the advantage of the modern F1 transmission.

While Williams' 1990s CVT was banned, the modern F1 gearbox that enables 2-millisecond shifts has fundamentally the same result, maintaining constant power output and shaving crucial nanoseconds between gear swaps. All of those hundredths of a second over thousands of shifts add up to over 10 seconds of advantage during the course of an entire race.

None of the trickery that enables such fast shifts would matter if it didn't come concurrently with advances in material science. Teams are 3D-printing titanium, then carving out small sections of that titanium and replacing them with carbon fiber to further reduce weight. Then F1 squads use a coating process on some parts called diamond-like carbon to reduce parts friction and increase wear life. All of these materials have to be used to withstand punishing heat while still offering exceptional strength-to-weight ratios.

That hand crafting as well as the gearbox's exotic materials explain its extreme cost. Still, that's a mere third of a million bucks, which is nothing compared to the $10 million to $15 million price of an entire F1 engine — even though they don't last long.

Probably what's more amazing about the transmission is that it's a stressed member. That means the gearbox not only has to withstand all the forces of constant rpm at up to 15,000 rpm and 500th-of-a-second gear changes, but it's also supporting the entire rear crash structure as well as the suspension. And the gearbox weighs a mere 88 pounds.

On top of all of that, F1 cars get a trick differential that's similar to what you'd want for your 4x4, since it can lock both rear wheels together in an instant to enable faster take-off. We'll suggest you might want to know the difference between a fully locking rear diff and a limited-slip differential before you decide to pavement-launch your not-F1 street car and detonate its non-3D-printed parts into smithereens.

#5738. $3.4 Billion — Anthropic Order for Gas Power Plants!

Wow, this is a nasty, dirty, polluting stunner I didn’t see until just now.

Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, has reportedly signed a $3.4 billion contract to buy gas-fired engines (power plants) from OnePWR Solutions, a Texas-based energy company. These gas power plants would be able to provide Anthropic’s AI data centers with an enormous amount of off-grid electricity — with the real cost being an enormous amount of air pollution and global warming emissions.

If you thought Anthropic was supposed to be “the good guy” in the AI industry, perhaps think again.

The Financial Times, which broke the news on this, says that this is the “largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab.” It’s this line from Futurism that really sums up my feelings: “It isn’t just symptomatic of a desperate race to secure the necessary utilities: it’s also one of the clearest signs yet that the AI industry has turned its back on the growing climate crisis in favor of pollution-spewing gas generators it’s installing across the globe.” Indeed. It’s one thing to be racing to be a leader in this field, but to turn to polluting, climate-destroying gas power plants instead of solar and wind power, that’s absolutely disappointing and — frankly — morally disgusting.

For the heck of it, to see what this company’s AI bot thought about the power choice it made, I decided to ask Claude “Are gas power plants harmful to our climate?” The response was as follows:

“Yes, though they’re less harmful than coal and more harmful than most alternatives.

“Bottom line: Gas is a cleaner fossil fuel, not a clean one. Its climate impact is best judged by what it replaces (coal vs. renewables) and by how tightly methane leaks are controlled. Carbon capture could reduce plant emissions, but it’s still costly and not widely deployed.”

So, yeah, when you’re choosing to buy $3.4 billion worth of gas power plants instead of renewable energy power plants, that is without a doubt going to be a horrible decision for our climate. I’m sure if I asked Claude about the risk humans race from climate change, the answer would not be uplifting. But I’m not going to go there. Instead, I’ll turn back to Futurism for this summary: “Researchers have found that the effects of AI on the environment are nothing short of devastating. And the prognosis for the future is grim. Last month, environmental nonprofit Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, wiping out nearly 15 years worth of greenhouse gas reduction efforts.”

Indeed — we’re facing drastic increases in emissions from the very dirty AI industry. The good news is people are already showing they’re fed up with AI data centers. Apparently, out of 41 ballot measures related to data centers that were up for a vote in the recent midterm elections, only one (1) went the way of the AI industry. That said, I don’t see investments in growth stopping right now, as is evidenced by this $3.4 billion gas engine order and OpenAI and others burning through billions of dollars a quarter.

#5737. Are Collectors Overpaying For These Japanese Sports Cars?

If you've been paying close attention to the collector car market in recent years, particularly since 2020, you've likely noticed that many golden era Japanese cars have started going for big bucks. Wealthy Gen X and millennial enthusiasts are pushing this nostalgia-fueled, Gran Turismo-inspired market well past what anyone might have thought possible in years gone by. With six-figure price tags no longer out of the ordinary, perhaps it's time to put a finger on the market's pulse and dig into the forces driving these massive prices. Are these cars really worth the spend, and will they continue to hold value into the future? It's tough to say for sure, but I'll give it my best shot.

Considering the comparative mass-market production numbers of some of these Japanese classics, maybe there isn't enough rarity for these cars to command the numbers they do. Then again, these are some of the greatest cars of their eras, and no automaker on the planet makes anything today that can compete on a level playing ground with the best of years gone by. Perhaps these values are just a combination of "They just don't make them like they used to" and "They aren't making any more of them."

At the end of the day, cars are only worth what someone is willing to pay for them, and in each of these cases it seems there are plenty of people willing to spend what it takes to buy them. Surely there are plenty of fools quick to part with their money, and there always will be. Some of these premium prices, however, are getting out of hand. Let's pump the brakes a little and get realistic about what collectors are actually getting for their cash.

I've spilled plenty of ink and burned plenty of internet pixels extolling the virtues of the flip-up-headlight Acura NSX. This is an incredible car and the driving experience is sublime. Perhaps the only problem with the NSX, especially now that Acura has started to reproduce many of the components needed to keep one alive, is that it's too good. The NSX doesn't have the sound or the fizz many of its Italian or German competitors from the era do. In that respect it's perhaps a little on the sterile side. It's so well-engineered that it just does everything you expect it to, which can't always be said of those competitors.

The long and short of this car is that I love it dearly, and I kind of understand why people are willing to spend deep into the hundreds of thousands of dollars for one. According to Hagerty, a #1 conscours-condition car is valued at a quarter of a million on the high end. This is borne out in recent Bring A Trailer auction results, with 10 red first-gen NSXes selling in October alone, ranging from $72,000 on up to $156,000 for a low-mile example. In many cases that's on par with, or even more than, Bring A Trailer's current sales prices of its contemporary Ferrari 348 competitors.

Between 1991 and the end of NSX production in 2004, U.S. sales added up to 8,733 cars, and about 18,000 worldwide. That's actually quite rare, all things considered, but there are always a few available. Buy a high-mile driver-grade NSX at a discount and keep driving it. These things are best once they've worn in a little.

When Datsun debuted the 240Z in the late 1960s as a bargain-priced competitor to the premium European sports cars of the day, it was wildly successful and helped cement the brand's place in the U.S. market. Why spend so much more for a Porsche 911 when a Datsun offered a similar level of performance and head-turning good looks? All these decades later, the 240Z is still a great low-priced vintage alternative to a vintage 911. Today the price gap is perhaps even higher between the German and the Datsun, though the maintenance and aftermarket parts support for both has continued to narrow.

Hagerty claims a #1 condition 240Z will command up to $181,000 at auction, but I don't think anything near that is even close to accurate. I've seen perfectly restored examples trade hands recently for as little as $50,000, and driver-grade units sell on Bring A Trailer every couple of weeks for between 20 and 45 grand. Whatever your budget, and whatever your stomach for tinkering, there's a 240Z out there for you.

Between 1969 and 1973 Nissan shipped 168,584 of these great little machines around the world. The vast majority of them (nearly 90%) ended up in the U.S., largely due to Europe's restrictive post-World War II trade embargoes. It's hard to call a 240Z overpriced, simply by dint of how many were built. There are plenty out there to sate collector demand, and prices reflect that. If you want one, go for it. As with any old car, beware of rusty, poorly restored cars, or any with a checkered past, as you'll pay more to fix one with issues than the premium for a nice one.

I am a Honda S2000 sycophant, convinced that this is the best driving experience that money can buy. If the Mazda Miata is always the answer, then the S2000 is the path to enlightenment. The early cars with an 8,800-rpm-redline 2.0-liter four-cylinder are pure driving joy. This is exhilaration, verve, and direct feel distilled to its most pure and uncut. If you've never driven one, you'll never understand it. Unlike the NSX, the S2000 is all fizz and very little usability. It's not great on the highway, isn't particularly comfortable, and has no room for anything. It was built to make you feel something, and that's pretty much all it can do. It's a real one-trick pony, but that trick is sublime.

Hagerty pegs a perfect condition AP1 at just over $64,000, up 22% from three years ago. Real-world sales on Bring A Trailer show buyers tapping out at $50,000 on the high end, with nice driver-grade examples down in the low 20s. If you look you might be able to find some in the high teens.

It's hard to call the S2000 rare, as Honda built over 110,000 of these little screamers across 11 years of production. I prefer the models built from 1999 to 2003; they're a little lighter, rev higher and the handling is more like balancing on the edge of a knife. Honda built far more AP1 versions of the car than it did the later 2.2-liter AP2 models, as 72,684 of the former made it out into the world. I don't think these will ever be purely collectible, just on the sheer number built, so don't pay a premium for a #1 example. Buy a nice driver and enjoy miles on twisty roads and track days.

As enthusiastic as I am about Honda's ripper S2000, I remain perplexed by the stratospheric growth of JZA80 Toyota Supra Turbo love. Aside from its role as the star of "The Fast And The Furious" and some highly modified examples, it's an entirely underwhelming ownership experience. Toyota designed the fourth-generation Supra around subframes, suspension, and drivetrain assemblies from the Z30-generation Soarer (sold in the U.S. as the Lexus SC), meaning it's a highly competent, comfortable grand tourer, but a sports car it is not. If you're after a high-speed long-legged highway cruiser, it's pretty great, but it doesn't really feel special to drive.

There's something to be said for above-average ergonomics and a practically indestructible engine wrapped in simple, attractive bodywork? Of course, but is it a driving experience worth up to $297,000? According to Hagerty, a concours condition Supra could bring that sum at auction. I can't recall having seen one trade hands for quite that much recently, but there are plenty of examples deep into the six figures, like this low-mile unit that went unsold on Bring A Trailer after a high bid of $209,000.

In every case I'd personally rather have a C5-generation Corvette, offering more power and more twisty-road-ready driving character for orders of magnitude less money. I'm excited that Japanese cars have been grabbing collector attention for the last couple of decades, but I'm positive you can find better cars offering more excitement behind the wheel than this. Japan, and indeed Toyota, has built better grand tourers and better sports cars (and cars that are better at both) since this car exited production.

The Acura Integra Type R is perhaps the car that best exemplifies the overpriced Japanese collector car. Don't get me wrong, this is a magnificent machine with legendary driving character, but at its core it's a pumped-up economy car. Even though it's possibly the best front-wheel-drive experience, and punches well above its weight, it seems downright offensive that these occasionally command six- figure price tags. It's got all the incredible characteristics of a fast Honda, including the reliability, tight steering, and wonderful shifter feel. It also comes with the downsides of a loud, buzzy interior, aesthetically underwhelming design, and a lack of low-end torque. It's a lot of fun on a track or a twisty road, but not a very nice daily driving experience.

According to the Hagerty valuation tool, an Integra Type R in concours condition can expect to bring around $99,000 at auction on the high end. This one seems to actually be underselling the highs of the Integra market, as Bring a Trailer results show. Last summer a low-mile ITR traded hands for $204,204. While nothing has reached that high since, a 19,000-mile example sold for $88,500 in October. Many of these cars have a checkered past, as Integras were once the most stolen car in America, so if you find one with high miles or a rebuilt title, you can probably get the same driving experience for a major discount. A driver-grade car seems to sell in the $20,000-to-$30,000 range.

If you're looking for a less expensive high-revving, great-handling front-wheel-drive economy-based car that works great when the road gets curvy, maybe try a Dodge Neon ACR instead. I put my money where my mouth is a couple years ago, and I never had any ITR jealousy.

There are plenty of other cars from Japan in this conversation, but I don't think this is an intrinsically Japanese collector car problem. In fact, cars from Japan tend to be overlooked by collectors, and have been for decades. There are plenty of reasons to buy a Japanese sports car, but as the market continues to trend upward, many enthusiasts are getting priced out of their dream cars. Still, some, perhaps even many, Japanese cars are still worth the money they command on the used market, especially in light of the lack of choices and driver connectivity in the new car market.

I typically don't like to talk about collector car values, because it continues to prop up the cars-as-commodities trading industry. Buy what you love and what makes you feel good, and drive the wheels off the thing. What's the point in having a car if you aren't going to drive it as it was meant to be driven? You don't get emotion or experience from storing value in your garage. Perhaps more than any other car-building nation, Japan understands experience and the interconnectedness between driver and machine.

If you're buying one of these cars because you're expecting it to go up in value and make you money, perhaps you'd be better served investing in the stock market or betting on the ponies. Cars are passion and craftsmanship, and they need to be driven to extract their full value to humanity. Go to a car show, a track day, or take one on a long road trip with friends. There are smiles to be found in those miles. Buy what makes you happy.

#5736. What The US Midterm Elections Mean For Climate Progress

People across the United States voted in record numbers in last week’s incredibly consequential election, which has completely changed the makeup of Congress for its new term beginning in January 2027. The success of our electoral processes—still underway—should not be taken for granted. It’s a win for democracy when millions of citizens peacefully claim their right to a government of, by, and for the people.

Will the Trump administration acknowledge voters’ repudiation of its destructive agenda and work in cooperation with this new Congress? That remains to be seen, and I’m not holding my breath. But there’s no question that the shift in Congress has significant implications for the administration’s ability to continue to ram through its anti-science, authoritarian agenda—including on climate and clean energy issues.

Energy affordability concerns, opposition to proliferating data centers, and anger at corruption and extreme economic inequality were undoubtedly driving forces in how people voted. While not everyone explicitly named climate change as a top issue (although many did put it in their top three), its fingerprints are all over the issues a majority of voters did name in polls.

If you care about addressing the high costs of electricity and gas, then you must reckon with the fact that this current fossil energy crisis, unleashed by the Trump administration’s war against Iran, is an extreme manifestation of the risks of fossil fuel dependence. The benefits of a transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy—renewable energy that the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked, further driving up costs for consumers—are tremendous. If you are deeply concerned about the rapid, unregulated build-out of data centers, you know that it comes with huge risks for communities related to climate, water, pollution, health, and electricity cost burdens. And it’s so clear that the Trump administration’s corruption, lies about climate science, and massive giveaways to fossil fuel polluters are leaving us all bearing the high costs of climate damages while large corporations and the president’s inner circle are raking in enormous profits.

Here’s another reality: regardless of politics, climate change is here, and science shows it’s rapidly worsening with the world’s imminent overshoot of 1.5°C of global warming. Communities are already experiencing deadly and costly climate impacts, including extreme heatwaves, catastrophic wildfires, record-breaking flooding, drought, accelerating sea level rise, intense ocean heat, irreversible loss of glaciers and ice sheets, stresses to critical ecosystems and more. These impacts are showing up in people’s daily lives—harming their health, destroying homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure, raising insurance premiums, hammering businesses, stressing water supplies, and threatening food security and affordability.

Climate change and clean energy are pocketbook issues. They are a lot more than that, of course. And climate change does not care if you live in a red state or a blue state. (One can ask if that is that even a relevant frame after an election that scrambled all conventional wisdom about “red” and “blue” dichotomies.)

Importantly, we will soon have a Congress where a majority accepts the scientific evidence on climate change. (Yes, I also wish we could take that for granted in 2026, but not in US politics, sadly.) That’s an important start and means we can advocate for policymakers to legislate based on the facts, instead of being stuck fighting disinformation and lies.

Here’s what this seismic “change election” could mean for action on climate change, some cautions about what likely won’t change right away, and what we’ll have to keep fighting for.

We will have to keep fighting back in courts to hold the Trump administration accountable for egregiously flouting the law. We’ve already had a major win in a lawsuit where the administration was found to be violating the Federal Advisory Committee Act in secretly setting up a ‘Climate Working Group’ stacked with climate contrarians to draft a sham science report, which the EPA then used to justify its proposal to gut the Endangerment Finding. We’ve also filed suit against the administration for repealing the Endangerment Finding, contrary to law, science, and the public interest.

On the international front, the Trump administration has shamefully exited the bedrock UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and that won’t change as long as it is in power. As I write from COP31 in Türkiye, the administration’s abandonment of global climate cooperation is very much on my mind; it’s crucial for the rest of the world to forge ahead regardless of the high stakes. There is a real risk that a beleaguered Trump administration will double down on its authoritarian ways and continue to find new ways to disrupt global climate progress and multilateral institutions. But Congress now has the power and responsibility to keep this reckless administration in check and ensure it is held accountable, at home and on the global stage.

“Change elections” come weighted with the hopes and dreams of many. As climate justice advocates, we know that policymakers have pushed off meaningful climate action far too long, and those failures are putting us all at profound risk. Yet, deep-pocketed fossil fuel interests, Big Tech, and other powerful entities continue to obstruct and delay action, still hold all too much sway over both parties in Congress, and we can expect their harmful tactics to ratchet up. So now it’s our responsibility to fight for what comes next, to make our shared dreams come true. Because those dreams of a safer, more just world for generations of young people to come must become reality.

#5735. At $12,500, Could This 2004 Nissan 350Z Be Your New Weekend Toy?

With low miles, a six-speed stick, and nothing-rhymes-with-it upholstery, today's Nice Price or No Dice 350Z convertible has a lot going for it as a fun-time car. Let's see how serious we feel about buying it at the seller's asking price.

It's been said—by old Shakespeare, no less—that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Value, it should likewise be noted, is also a subjective concept. One person's fancy restaurant burger is another's meal budget for an entire week. Mmmm, ramen.

When it comes to cars and trucks, value is rooted not only in price, but also in perceived usefulness and desirability. The seller of the 1999 Ford Expedition XLT that we looked at last Friday asked only $2,600 for it, a mere pittance in today's market. We had to consider, however, not just the dollars, but the desirability of a large SUV like that. Not everybody is keen on something that gets around 12 mpg around town and eyes compact parking spaces the same way Santa looks at skinny jeans. For many of you, that price was too hard to beat, regardless of potential pitfalls. The result was an overwhelming 89% 'Nice Price' win.

Have you looked at a weather report lately? According to meteorologists (which, by the way, is the coolest job title out there next to automotive journalist), North America is about to experience a wet and wild winter, thanks to the Super El Niño now taking up residence in the Pacific. Stormy weather? Wet, maybe slushy roads? That means this might not be the best time to consider buying a RWD, convertible sports car.

Being a community of naysayers, though, and those who forge our own path (usually sideways or backward, spraying a rooster tail of dirt and grass), that's just what we're going to consider. The object of our attention, this 2004 Nissan 350Z convertible, is sufficiently unique in a desirable way to warrant our immediate attention, even if using it to its full potential and driver enjoyment might have to wait until the drier days of Spring and Summer.

Okay, so what's to like about this 350Z? Well, for starters, it's a front-mid engine two-seater with a 287-horsepower naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 under the hood, mated to a six-speed manual. That's a spicy meatball right there. Then there's the convertible top. Yes, not everyone likes unlimited headroom and showing off a Rogaine prescription for all to see, but some do.

As added enticements, the seller claims that the car is completely factory-stock and has a mere 61,000 miles on the clock. That's less than 3,000 miles a year. What a waste!

The reason given for the meager miles is that the car has been used exclusively as a weekend warrior for the past few years, sitting out the work week entirely. As a result, the car is said to be in excellent condition, with a smooth-shifting gearbox and a fuss-free engine. With so few miles under its belt, we have to wonder if it's even on its original brake pads.

Another reason to check out this Z is its almost-new appearance. Painted in dark silver metallic—as were, it seems, 90% of these cars—this Z looks clean and well-kept. The black fabric top is in equally good condition, as are the factory alloys. The tires wrapping those have plenty of tread depth but are cheap-seats Phantom HRX meats which, while not terrible, were probably chosen with the car's sale in mind.

This Z's party piece, however, is its two bucket seats. The rest of the cabin is dullsville black plastic, but the seats, cosseting, modestly-bolstered affairs, are orange-dyed leather with charcoal mesh insets. Those are in great shape, happily showing no wear whatsoever in the pictures. Equally up to snuff are the steering wheel wrap and shift knob, two more leather surfaces. The car has a full complement of comfort and convenience features—cruise, climate control, power windows and locks, etc.—and all are said to work as they should. The cabin also has the added, odd benefit of a factory Bose stereo with both a CD and cassette player built right in.

So far, we've established that this Z puts a lot on the table for an enthusiast to enjoy. Two final incentives: it also has a clean title and the seller's insistence that this is a collectible model.

Known in America as the "Z" or "Z car," Nissan's venerated sports car carried the wonderful Fairlady name in its home market. Over the years, changing market priorities have stunted the Z's U.S. sales. While Nissan has dutifully stuck it out and still sells an updated version of this car today, when was the last time you saw one on the road? In fact, while the company has introduced the new 2027 models, its website still touts that "last year's model year Nissan Z is still available." How sad is that? Maybe the $45K price tag plays a role.

This older, but claimed "like-new" Z asks a far lower $12,500, and it's now time for you all to weigh in on whether that's a fair price or not. What do you think? Is this well-equipped, fantastically upholstered 350Z worth $12,500 as presented in its ad? Or does that price have you thinking about going Rogue?

#5734. 313 kW Rooftop Solar System at Virginia Elementary Will Save $581,000 in Energy Costs

Roanoke City Schools to Add 313 kW Solar Power System

Staunton, VA — Secure Solar Futures, a provider of on-site clean energy to schools, local governments, and businesses, will build a 313-kilowatt solar power system installed at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, VA. Construction of the system is expected later this year at no capital cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement with Secure Solar Futures. Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, a subsidiary of Pardee Resources Company, will provide the majority of the capital for the solar system.

A total of 531 bi-facial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, TX, will be installed on the rooftop of the school located at 3142 Preston Avenue, NW, and will offset 67% of the power used by the school annually.

In its first year, the school’s solar system will produce 421 megawatt hours of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes and provide environmental benefits by avoiding 371 metric tons of carbon pollution, which is equal to the emissions produced by 87 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles, or the carbon sequestered by 372 acres of U.S. forests, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Under the Power Purchase Agreement, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, together with its partner Secure Solar Futures, will own, operate, and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

During the term of the Power Purchase Agreement, Preston Park Elementary School will save $581,000 in net avoided costs for electricity. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s 35- to 40-year productive lifespan.

Roanoke City Public Schools (RCPS) is an urban school division in Roanoke, Virginia, serving a pre-K through 12th grade population of approximately 14,000 students. RCPS provides an inclusive and equitable, student-centered culture that empowers lifelong learning. Through meaningful, relevant, and engaging learning opportunities, we will empower all students to dream, excel, and meet their full potential to benefit our city and its citizens. The division has 17 elementary schools, five middle schools, two high schools, and five program locations, including the Roanoke Valley Governor’s School for Science & Technology and two career and technical education centers. Visit www.rcps.info for additional information.

#5733. Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas

Fossil fuels are slowly beginning to lose their grip on the global transportation sector, with one key omission: rocket fuel. The rocket fuel conundrum has earned an uptick in attention in recent years, now that rocket launches, once rare, are becoming as commonplace as rush hour traffic. The Elon Musk venture SpaceX, for example, is building new natural gas pipelines in order to produce its own methane-based propellant, needed to sustain the launch of many thousands of rockets in the coming years.

Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

With its future volume of launch operations in mind, SpaceX aims to exercise as much control as possible over its fuel supply. The company is investing in its own natural gas pipelines and on-site fuel production facilities to help ensure that the taps don’t run dry, though it still relies on the gas industry to find the stuff and bring it up from the ground.

SpaceX has already been sucking up a copious amount of natural gas for its existing operations in Texas and Florida. “SpaceX (SPCX) is emerging as one of the largest new customers for natural gas,” reported the oil and gas analytics firm East Daley in October.

“Unlike Falcon 9, which burns rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen, Starship creates a direct link between launch activity and natural gas consumption. SPCX plans to process and liquefy pipeline gas into liquid methane to fuel the rockets,” East Daley elaborates.

As described by East Daley, the SpaceX subsidiary Coastal Connect Services is planning a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline to hook up SpaceX operations in Cape Canaveral, Florida with existing infrastructure jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer.

Meanwhile, at the company’s launch site and newly incorporated (as of 2025) City of Starbase in Cameron County, Texas, plans are in motion for SpaceX affiliate Lone Star Mineral Development to connect the new 8-mile “Starpipe” natural gas pipeline with another 145-mile pipeline currently being built by the firms WhiteWater, Enbridge, and MPLX. Starpipe is expected to begin shuttling natural gas into Starbase Texas early next year.

The two pipeline projects come alongside word that SpaceX has nailed down approvals for parts of a new $100 billion project that expands the company’s US footprint into another combination city-and-launch-site under the name of Starbase, Louisiana. The new city will presumably also require a reliable supply of natural gas for on-site rocket fuel production.

For the record, Starbase, Louisiana is not part of the educational non-profit organization STARBASE Louisiana, an affiliate of the national STARBASE program of the US Department of Defense, aimed at stimulating interest in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) topics among 5th grade students. The Louisiana branch of STARBASE is located Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier Parish, in the northwestern part of the state.

Starbase, Louisiana will take up 125,000 acres of land at Pecan Island in a marshy region along the southern coast in Vermilion Parish, where plans are being laid for 30 launches per day. More than a dozen launch towers will eventually sprout up at the site, where the operation will include producing rocket fuel.

If you’ve gotten wind of the project under the name “Osprey,” you’re not dreaming. The new city was reportedly code-named “Project Osprey” during initial discussions with public officials. As described by the Gulf State News affiliate WWNO (New Orleans Public Radio) on November 11, Project Osprey was shrouded in secrecy during the initial negotionas, with “dozens” of local officials signing non-disclosure agreements that limited what they could say about the project.

The Osprey code name also reportedly enabled Vermilion Parish officials to sidestep public participation in ostensibly public hearings on the Starbase, Louisiana project earlier this year. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry finally let the cat out of the bag in a public announcement in August. Local residents and the nonprofit organization Vermillion Citizens coalition have already filed a lawsuit against the project, alleging that parish officials approved parts of Starbase, Louisiana in violation of the state’s Open Public Meetings Law.

If and when shovels hit the ground on Starbase, Louisiana, the Trump administration is taking steps to help ensure that natural gas producers in the US come through with the goods — not just for SpaceX, of course, although the firm has become a market-mover in the gas industry as noted by East Daley.

On November 10, for example, the US Department of Energy announced the finishing touches on a $480 million loan in support of Project Elkhorn, an endeavor under the umbrella of the oil and gas firm Arena Energy. Project Elkhorn covers the modernization of 22 existing platforms off the Louisiana coast — coincidentally or not, the same state that expects to host the new Starbase city.

Arena launched in 1999 with a focus on revitalizing mature oil and gas fields. According to the Energy Department, Project Elkhorn will ramp natural gas production up to 77 million cubic feet per day at peak production among the 22 platforms, alongside up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day. By way of contrast, the 22 platforms currently produce 30,000 barrels of oil per day. Over the lifespan of Project Elkhorn, the collective total is expected to add 25 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to the US fossil energy roster.

As CEO of the leading EV maker Tesla, Elon Musk has earned his share of credit for rescuing electric cars from the dustbin of automotive obscurity and vaulting them into the mainstream mobility market of today — if not so much here in the US, then certainly overseas. Musk’s other ventures, on the other hand, threaten to offset, if not override, whatever sustainability gains are to be made from EVs.

In addition to SpaceX, Musk’s xAI data centers have also contributed to spiking demand for natural gas. Last year word dropped that Musk’s Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee trucked in approximately three dozen industrial-sized gas generators to power the site, at least 15 of which were already in operation without an air quality permit. The Southern Environmental Law Center has been among those raising the alarm over toxic emissions from the generators, which lack the pollution controls required of permanent power plants.

Natural gas also factors into a new data center planned for the SpaceX-backed City of Starbase, Texas, which sits adjacent to Brownsville. The city of Brownsville recently imposed a temporary moratorium on new data center construction. According to ABC News affiliate KVUE and other sources, earlier this year Elon Musk asked Brownsville officials to de-annex a parcel of land at its outskirts, evidently in order to building a $24 billion data center at the site along with a new gas-fired power plant for a new data center to be located in Starbase. The request was granted, enabling the project to skirt around the Brownsville moratorium.

Starbase city officials are scheduled to conduct a public hearing on the new data center on December 9, where presumably they will decide whether or not the project can make due with gas generators until a full gas power plant with appropriate pollution controls can materialize.

Over and above the rocket fuel issue, grassroots activists, environmental organizations, and researchers have been raising the alarm over the impact of Starbase in Texas for years, tracking significant harm to local public recreation resources as well as wildlife habitats. Similar concerns have surfaced around SpaceX’s plans for Starbase, Louisiana.

Of course, nobody seriously expects the whole domestic rocket business to stop in its tracks. The issue is one of mitigating climate and biodiversity risks, developing projects that avoid pummeling vulnerable communities with additional public health risks, and investing in more sustainable options including alternative rocket fuels.

Keep an eye on the aviation industry for some hints at the future of sustainable propellants. Airline stakeholders have been focusing on SAF, generally meaning a bio-based equivalent of kerosene jet fuel. However, the going has been slow, and it’s even slower in the field of propellants. The European Space Agency, for example, has been exploring green propellants for space operations for 25 years, with little to show for its efforts.

More recently, though, aviation stakeholders have begun turning to the emerging electrofuels or “solar fuels” industry, meaning fuels synthesized from captured carbon and green hydrogen, with solar and other renewables powering the operation. The green hydrogen industry has been struggling for traction, but signs of scaleup have finally emerged, with e-kerosene jet fuel in play along with green hydrogen. Honda, for one, is envisioning a fleet of reusable rockets propelled by renewable fuels, and at least two Chinese firms are also working the reusable rocket angle.

Image: SpaceX is among the industrial-scale consumers of natural gas adding more pipes to the nation’s sprawling network of gas pipelines, which the startup needs to ensure a steady supply of fuel for its growing fleet of rockets (courtesy of US Energy Information Agency).

#5732. What's The First Thing You'd Change If Stellantis Made You Its CEO?

Stellantis is making moves again, this time promoting Tim Kuniskis from merely being the head of its American brands and SRT division to also being its U.S. chief commercial officer. That means Tim's now in charge of the entire dealer network, as well as retail and fleet sales. Since he's in the C-suite, it probably comes with a big raise, too, unlike the promotions that regular people get in America.

Kuniskis isn't European, and it's hard to imagine Stellantis putting an American in charge of its entire corporation, but if anyone could do it, it would be Tim. He's made them a lot of money stuffing big, dumb engines into cars that make big, dumb horsepower, and even if they aren't your cup of tea, it's hard to get too mad at the guy that gave us the Hellcat.

It would be hard to Hellcat all of Stellantis's European brands, but personally, I'd be ok with Fiat building a 700-horsepower 500e. I assume Stellantis CEO Tim Kuniskis would prefer V8s, but if the Fiat's already electric, could he resist building a version that makes big, dumb power? I don't think he could. Because he's Tim Kuniskis, and he likes to go fast.

Similar things could be said about other executives. No matter who hires Johan de Nysschen, you know any good names in the lineup are about to become alphanumeric gibberish. No matter how many vehicles Rivian builds, don't expect RJ Scaringe to offer animal leather as an upholstery option. I bet you have some pretty strong beliefs about the best way to run an automaker, too.

So if you became the next CEO of Stellantis, what's the first change you'd make? Remember, you aren't just in charge of U.S. brands. You're the boss of the whole corporation. Maybe you'd do something about Chrysler, but maybe not. You could always start with a brand we don't get here. Do you have a plan to save Lancia? I'd be willing to be someone here wants to save Lancia.

No need to type out a whole business plan. Just share the first thing you'd do as CEO of Stellantis. Personally? I'd quit. Being any kind of automotive executive seems like a giant headache, and I don't think even a wheelbarrow full of money would make that headache go away. Regardless of what your answer is, though, be sure to let us know down in the comments.
