#5718. Ford Employee Allegedly Funneled 'Millions' In Factory Parts To A Detroit Auto Shop

Generally, I don't recommend stealing from your employer, and if you're going to do it, try to be discreet at the very least. Unfortunately, one Ford employee didn't heed that advice, and now he and three other folks are in a heap of trouble. For six weeks in the spring of 2025, Stratec Auto in Detroit received deliveries of brand new parts straight from Ford's Rouge Complex every Saturday night... until Ford security caught on.

Now, the four men are charged with stealing well over $80,000 in parts from the Dearborn, Michigan, factory, Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy told Automotive News. 35-year-old Wissam Faraj reportedly took parts from the Rogue factory where he worked, to give them to 63-year-old Badr Kahil and his sons, 25-year-old Aiman and 36-year-old Firas. The men allegedly sold the stolen parts through the repair shop and on eBay.

One of the Kahils would simply place an order for parts with Faraj for him to steal from Ford. From there, he'd simply take them and deliver the parts to the shop. Worthy described the scheme as "lucrative, shameless and absolutely illegal."

Ford began its investigation after other employees at the plant noticed parts were going missing, which isn't something that typically happens. From there, The Blue Oval notified Dearborn police, who arranged a sort of sting operation. Officers set up a controlled purchase for more parts to catch the men in the act. They also looked at thousands of texts, emails, photos, videos, and various online accounts, according to FOX 2 Detroit.

It's actually possible that the value of the stolen parts could end up being significantly greater than what was listed in the charges, because it's so hard to track everything down. Worthy pointed to a text message from Faraj that referenced one order for 128 sets of headlights that totaled $22,400 on its own. It's very possible that the number could reach into the "millions," FOX 2 reports. Worthy described it as "a very large amount of money."

Here's what Ford said about the matter in a statement to FOX 2 Detroit:

"Ford's Global Security team launched a thorough investigation after notification of suspected theft and unauthorized sale of company parts at two manufacturing facilities. While we do not comment on individual personnel matters, the team conducted a comprehensive review of the incident and implemented corrective actions to strengthen security measures at our sites. The company will continue to work with local authorities throughout the investigation."

Faraj, unsurprisingly, was fired in 2025.

#5717. NAED Unveils PV-1 PECVD-V, a U.S.-Engineered Vertical Deposition Platform Built for 96,000-Wafer-per-Hour Tandem Solar Manufacturing

Patent-pending vertical PECVD/PVD architecture doubles wafer throughput over NAED’s previous platform and is designed to produce perovskite/HJT tandem cells targeting 30% efficiency

NAED Energy Holding Inc. (“NAED”), the U.S. aerospace, engineering, and utility-energy company behind NAED Nexus Core™, last week unveiled PV-1 PECVD-V, a vertical in-line deposition platform for high-volume solar cell manufacturing. PV-1 combines plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) and physical vapor deposition (PVD) on a single shared-carrier line. It is designed for a throughput of 96,000 wafers per hour, double the 48,000 wafers per hour of NAED’s previous XL-class platform.

In PV-1, wafers travel upright on a shared carrier through every PECVD and PVD stage. To reach the second side of the wafer, the system never flips the substrate: the entire carrier is lifted and turned 180 degrees as a unit. This keeps wafers seated in the same carrier from first deposition to last, cutting direct wafer handling between process steps. The PV-1 production line, its 180-degree carrier turn, its wafer-retention carrier, and the T2X tandem cell are the subject of pending U.S. patent applications assigned to NAED Energy Holding Inc. NAED’s intellectual property portfolio has been independently appraised at $179 million under an ASC 820 Level 3 fair-value methodology, as of November 11, 2026.

PV-1 was engineered from the start for tandem solar. The full line, including perovskite top-cell process tools, is designed to produce NAED’s T2X two-terminal perovskite/heterojunction (HJT) tandem cell, which targets 30% cell efficiency. NAED plans to bring T2X cells to both terrestrial and space solar markets, alongside a family of glass-glass T2X modules starting at 600 W.

Every PV-1 tool is designed in-house by NAED and machined in its own aerospace-grade CNC shop in the United States. The first six of PV-1’s thirteen process tools are complete, and the remaining seven are in production. Engineering and design for the full PV-1 line and its production facility are complete.

“Going vertical, let us double throughput and build the line around tandem cells from day one, rather than retrofitting tandem onto a platform designed for something else,” said Malcom Longair, Media & Development Lead, NAED Energy Holding Inc. “With PV-1, manufacturers anywhere in the world can reserve U.S.-engineered deposition equipment built for the next generation of solar cells.”

NAED is now opening reservations for PV-1 production tool slots to solar cell manufacturers in the United States and internationally. Manufacturers can request specifications and reserve a slot at NAED. energy or through the media and partnership contact below.

UnitedHealth releases independent audit of its medical policy development practices" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Over the past year, UnitedHealth Group has conducted a series of independent reviews of its practices as part of a broader turnaround effort at the company.

The healthcare giant released the last of these analyses on Thursday, digging into the processes it uses to establish medical policies. The reviews were conducted by FTI Consulting and Rubrum Advising, a provider-led firm with expertise in medical coverage policies.

While the auditors dove into the processes the insurer uses to develop its medical policies, the report doesn't examine the application of those polices and any impact on coverage denials, an area where UnitedHealthcare has drawn significant public scrutiny.

The report concluded the company's methods "were strong overall and that the medical policy development process reflected numerous best practices."

For instance, UnitedHealthcare's Medical Policy team uses a structured and standardized process to establish medical policies, rooted in evidence-based and stakeholder-informed approaches. Clinical evidence comes from nationally recognized authorities, and epidemiologists play a key role in the review process, per the report.

In addition, the analysts concluded that the team is well-staffed with qualified workers and operates under a strong governance model. Medical policies are built "using systematic evidence review, evidence-based tools and industry best practices," and UnitedHealthcare is transparent about posting these policies and making updates.

All policies are reviewed at least once per year, the report found.

CEO Stephen Hemsley said in a letter to investors that the company will continue to conduct such analyses.

"We will continue to subject key practices across UnitedHealth Group to independent review, share results publicly and make changes where needed," Hemsley wrote. "This work reflects our broader commitment to transparency, accountability and continuous improvement."

While the report concluded that overall processes in place at UnitedHealth were up to snuff, the consultants did offer multiple areas of improvement for the company, too. For instance, the analysts said that the team could improve its documentation practices, including how it details criteria for policy development.

Plus, the report suggests that UnitedHealthcare review how it documents vetting criteria for internal and external subject matter experts. The company could also do more to formally document training and education for members of its governance committee.

Medical policy documents can be lengthy and complex, so the consultants recommended the insurer consider developing a template that standardizes the written format for each policy, which would make it easier to understand. For example, the template could make it easier to connect the evidence summary to the coverage rationale.

"While these gaps do not diminish the overall strength of the program, addressing them would further enhance transparency and consistency and provide opportunities for continued refinement," the analysts wrote.

#5715. FDA OKs First Drug for Primary Membranous Nephropathy

— Anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab lands indication on strength of MAJESTY trial

The FDA has once again expanded the label for the B-cell depleter obinutuzumab (Gazyva), this time to include treatment of primary membranous nephropathy.

The new indication, announced by the agency on Friday, stipulates use of the anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody to induce remissions of proteinuria in adults at risk for progression from primary membranous nephropathy. It marks the first approved agent for the type of autoimmune kidney disease where off-label options had become standard.

"Primary membranous nephropathy is a rare kidney disease caused by immune system attack on the glomeruli, which are the tiny filters in the kidneys that clean waste products from the blood," the FDA stated. "The glomeruli become inflamed and damaged, leaking large amounts of protein into the urine. Patients can develop high cholesterol, high blood pressure, severe swelling, fatigue, kidney failure, and other complications."

Phase III trial data from MAJESTY underpinned the approval, showing superior proteinuria remission rates with obinutuzumab versus tacrolimus, an immunosuppressive drug used off-label for the disease.

In the open-label trial, 37% of the patients assigned to obinutuzumab achieved a complete remission at 2 years -- defined as a urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio of ≤0.3 amid a stable estimated glomerular filtration rate -- versus just 6% of those on tacrolimus (P<0.001).

The percentage of patients with either a complete or partial remission was also higher in the obinutuzumab group (51% vs 13%, P<0.001), and benefits appeared consistent across prespecified subgroups.

Common side effects with obinutuzumab in the trial included infusion-related reactions (38%) and upper respiratory tract infections (14%).

Primary membranous nephropathy has typically been managed with off-label drugs, including agents that block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, immunosuppressive agents, glucocorticoids, cytotoxic medications, and calcineurin inhibitors. Rituximab, a first-generation anti-CD20 antibody, has also shown benefit.

In patients without diabetes, the autoimmune kidney disease is the leading cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.

Obinutuzumab now carries three indications in kidney disease, following approvals earlier this year for childhood-onset idiopathic nephrotic syndrome and last year for active lupus nephritis, based on results of the REGENCY study. The biologic is also approved for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and follicular lymphoma, while systemic lupus erythematosus may be its next indication.

The label for obinutuzumab carries boxed warnings for hepatitis B virus reactivation and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The warnings and precautions section also notes potential risks for infusion-related reactions, hypersensitivity reactions, serious infections (live-virus vaccines should be avoided while using the drug), neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and embryo-fetal toxicity.

#5714. '93 Porsche 911 RS Americas Cost Less Than Carrera 2s New, But Collectors Reversed That

Buyers looking to take home a Porsche 911 in 2026 are faced with a big bill, no matter the grade. After all, the 911 is a high-end sports car, not a value-focused commuter. The cheapest way into a 911 today is via the Carrera, which commands $137,850 including its $2,350 destination fee. Expenses quickly swell further up the ladder; the Carrera T demands an additional $12,500, the Carrera S $20,700, while the track-focused GT3 commands an outlay of $238,150.

We test-drove a GT3 RS in 2022 and found it both bewitching and bewildering, so understand this: we appreciate what's on offer at the upper end of the 911 model range, but the GT3 is undeniably expensive. However, Porsche hasn't always positioned its lightweight, performance-oriented 911s at the top of its price ladder.

When the RS America debuted back for the 1993 model year during the 964's reign, it actually sat as the cheapest grade in the whole lineup. It set buyers back $55,525 ($128,411 today), including destination fee, while the Carrera 2 carried an MSRP of $65,715 ($151,978). Sure, it had no more power than a base Carrera 2, but it was about 80 pounds lighter (depending on factory options), had no rear seats, did without much sound deadening, and had a wheel and suspension setup tailored to the track. Fast-forward a few decades, and the pricing picture for these two models has changed.

Porsche's initial pricing for its RS America and Carrera 2 likely made sense to both the automaker and its customers at the time. After all, the Carrera 2 offered many features the RS America did not, such as power steering, door bins, those rear seats, and a motorized rear spoiler rather than a fixed ducktail spoiler. However, as time progressed, collectors have become increasingly drawn to stripped-down models with more limited runs, like the RS America. Porsche only produced 701 examples of its RS America over two years, and the car's initial $10,000 "discount" is nowhere to be seen today.

Today, Classic tells us that the market benchmark for this model now sits at almost $175,000, a world away from that original $55,525 MSRP, and particularly desirable examples hold list prices exceeding $300,000. That's incredible for what was once considered the value model, even if it's only scratching the surface of what can be commanded by the 964, as evidenced by the 1993 model's $2.8 million market benchmark.

By contrast, the Carrera 2 could not be further from these figures. For example, the benchmark figure provided by Classic for 1993 manual coupes sits at $112,993. Targa and Cabriolets command even less, with benchmark valuations sitting at $93,750.

Porsche did not bring its true European market 964 Carrera RS to the U.S., instead introducing the RS America as a way of quenching the U.S.' thirst for a more performance-oriented 911. The new model featured the standard 3.6-liter mill, which for the '93 model year offered 247 horsepower and 228 pound-feet; nothing to shout about today, but plenty enough for the early '90s. It also made use of the Carrera 2's standard G50 5-speed manual transmission, and the only performance-minded option available to buyers of the RS America was a limited-slip differential.

In order to transition the Carrera 2 from comfy cruiser into capable performer, the RS America was equipped with Brembo calipers, an M030 Sports Suspension Package, powered Recaro seats, and 17-inch alloy wheels. After Porsche retired its RS America, other markets benefited from the lightweight 993 Carrera RS and GT2, but North America received neither. It wouldn't be until the 996.2 GT3 (2004 model year debut) that a true lightweight special again arrived on U.S. shores. The 996 is supposedly better than the 993 when it comes to driving characteristics, but ultimately, it's Porsche's earlier air-cooled specials like its RS America and later 993 cars that see collectors reaching deeper into their pockets.

The company says the suite will “continue to evolve to best support clinicians through the complex affordability and coverage landscape.”

The American Medical Association (AMA) adopted a policy on Monday that declares AI can be used to aid physicians and assist with clinical tasks, but cannot be granted licensure, professional titles or certifications to practice medicine.

Moreover, the organization said it will advocate for legislation that establishes a framework for physician oversight of AI clinical-decision making. The organization also is calling for protections for physicians when AI tools cause patient harm.

AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement that "patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care."

"Physicians also need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team," Underwood said.

Identity verification company Clear launched Monday two integrations within the Epic Toolbox, which will allow health systems to verify outside providers and prescribing clinicians.

The deal pairs Ellipsis's "emotionally intelligent" AI voice care manager, Sage, with Kouper's native EHR integrations and longitudinal patient maps to deliver continuous, connected patient care, according to the companies.

Ellipsis Health works with seven of the top 20 health plans in the U.S. and leading academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks.

Sage is used by nine of the top 15 U.S. health plans and has delivered up to 7x ROI for customers, the company said.

Sage is powered by a patented "empathy engine" trained on over 3 million labeled clinical conversations. It analyzes vocal cues in real time to assess emotional signals and adapt its interactions. Through phone and text, Sage supports care management tasks including enrollment, clinical assessments, medication adherence and post-discharge follow-up.

Kouper’s team is joining Ellipsis. Both companies will continue serving existing customers under their respective brands while developing a combined product roadmap, with new offerings for health systems expected in the months ahead.

Kouper brings critical infrastructure for making that possible inside health systems. By combining their native integrations and longitudinal patient maps with Sage’s emotional intelligence, we can help care teams extend their reach and deliver more continuous, personalized support.”

#5712. Mobile Energy Hubs: How Chery Auto’s Smart Energy Ecosystem Supports the Development of Smart Cities Worldwide

WUHU, China — Following the 2026 Chery International User Summit, Chery Auto is pressing ahead with its new energy ecosystem strategy. Entering the Globalization 3.0 phase, the company is deploying a mix of energy solutions to meet mobility energy needs around the world. As electric vehicles integrate with power grids, Chery Auto is developing a smart energy ecosystem that transforms new energy vehicles (NEVs) into dispatchable distributed mobile energy nodes, supporting grid management, sustainable urban development, and local energy resource utilization.

Unlike conventional charging, which can increase peak demand, V2G offers a flexible alternative. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) enables bidirectional flow, allowing vehicles to store off-peak electricity and return power during peak demand. For users, this creates opportunities to participate in energy management and potentially generate value. With participation depending on commercial feasibility and user confidence, Chery Group’s global user base exceeding 21 million provides a foundation for V2G deployment.

Chery Auto is validating its energy ecosystem across homes, communities and industrial parks. Its household Energy Cube integrates solar, storage and bidirectional charging to support electricity supply during exceptional conditions. In Wuhu, a large-scale AC V2G demonstration station enables private vehicles to support grid management through onboard chargers with limited modifications. In Spain, an industrial park microgrid uses green electricity to reduce energy costs, fossil fuel dependence, and carbon emissions.

Chery Auto’s Volt-dragon Ultra-Fast Charging technology targets 500 km of range in five minutes. Its hybrid engine has achieved 48.57% thermal efficiency, while the planned Rhino S solid-state battery targets 400 Wh/kg energy density. Chery’s Rhino Battery prioritizes fast charging, longevity and safety, addressing battery degradation and thermal management concerns associated with V2G charging cycles.

Chery Auto is developing modular solar, storage, charging, and V2G solutions tailored to regional infrastructure. In Europe, electricity markets provide opportunities for distributed energy participation. Mature markets integrate vehicles into grid management, while regions with weaker infrastructure can prioritize microgrids before introducing V2G.

Through applications spanning households, communities, and industrial parks, Chery Auto is extending automotive-grade engineering into energy infrastructure. Its approach supports distributed energy networks using locally generated electricity and managing energy flows, positioning Chery to participate in future smart cities.

#5711. This Ultra Rare WWII-Era Mobile Emergency Room Could Be Your Next Money-Pit Project

Before World War II, America was on the move via planes, trains, cars and, most importantly for this article, buses. Greyhound was so successful at the time, it was trying to take transport to the skies. Naturally, other bus coach companies sprang up to compete, which is how this Pink-ish Pony Cruiser came into existence. Listed on Bring a Trailer, this classic bus just wants to keep on dancing on the road, and you could be the one to give it a beautiful second life.

Pony Cruisers were 16-18 passenger buses made by Michigan coachbuilder Kalamazoo Coaches in the 1940s. The company became Unifab Corporation in the 1950s, and still operates today in nearby Portage, Michigan. Kalamazoo Coaches produced about 625 of these Pony Cruisers. Three of them were turned into Mobile Emergency Room Units, like the patina-covered bus pictured above. Designed for President Franklin Delano Roosevelt's U.S. Office of Civilian Defense, they were meant for practical applications during air raids, industrial disasters, and battlefield-adjacent triage. Rather important duties after the 1941 bombing of Pearl Harbor. The units were sold after the war, with this particular unit going to Snyder Ambulance Company where it was used until 1951. After that, it was parked and slowly turned into a time capsule complete with unused gauze, medicine bottles and plasma cans.

Pony Cruisers like this bus were built on a Ford commercial chassis, powered by a 239 cubic-inch flathead V8 paired with a three-speed manual transmission. The speedometer is said to top out at around 100 mph. BaT shows an odometer at around 19,000 miles, although real mileage is unknown.

The rear is a little mobile hospital complete with cabinets, a 120-volt outlet, patient tables clad in brown vinyl padding and other medical equipment. It will also come with four rolling gurneys. It looks like nearly everything is there, just in roughish shape.

The faded red-and-white paint still wears a faint bit of the "Snyder Ambulance Service Hospital" lettering on the sides. It features 18" steel wheels, front and rear spotlights, period-suited porthole-style side windows, and rear barn doors.

BaT mentions there was no serial number found on the bus, so this historical monument on wheels will be sold with a bill of sale. Getting a title might be the least of your worries. Attempting a full restoration on this American relic will not be an easy feat. What it would be though is a nod to preserving a massive part of America's past, especially its WWII history in a time of great uncertainty. That and preserving what little bits of non-Detroit automotive history are left about the U.S. as that also slowly disappears with age and time.

#5709. COP31 Leaders’ Summit Spotlights Electrification & Transition Away from Fossil Fuels

Antalya, Türkiye — The COP31 Leaders’ Summit concluded today, with several new announcements and speeches from heads of state and the UN Secretary-General. Developments included country endorsements of the COP Presidency’s 35×35 electrification pledge, growing support for the transition away from fossil fuels, and new pledges from philanthropies to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, among others.

Following is a statement from Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO, World Resources Institute:

“One message came across loud and clear from world leaders: climate action has shifted from an environmental movement to a core economic and security imperative. The conversation is moving beyond high-level commitments to the practical challenges of how to transition away from fossil fuels while supporting workers and communities and how to put entire economies on a cleaner, more resilient path.

“Electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels rightly took center stage. These are two vital, intertwined goals, and progress on one must reinforce the other. Early support for the 35×35 electrification pledge is encouraging, but many more countries need to endorse it and turn their commitments into credible national plans backed by concrete policies and investment.

“President Lula deserves credit for keeping the transition away from fossil fuels at the top of the international agenda and delivering a global roadmap that countries can adapt to their own circumstances. Australia and Türkiye now have an opportunity to lead by example, putting forward their own transition plans and encouraging others to follow.

“Vulnerable countries delivered an equally clear message: access to affordable finance is critical to them implementing their climate ambition. High borrowing costs and unsustainable debt are holding back investment in the very countries that need it most. With the $1.3 trillion finance goal established, the focus is shifting to how all sources of finance can work together to deliver investment at scale and how we ensure affordable capital reaches those who need it most. There are encouraging signs, including an influx of pledges from philanthropies for the Brazil-initiated Tropical Forests Forever Facility.

“Adaptation and early warning systems received much-needed attention after a year of crushing heatwaves, fires, and floods. But that attention now needs to turn to the investment in systemic resilience as the best way to make economies and societies stronger and improve people’s lives. Building more resilient cities was a major focus and will take deep collaboration between national governments, cities, and states. Cities are on the front lines of delivering the climate solutions and essential services that make people’s lives better, and demonstrating these benefits is critical to accelerating the transition. Local leaders are on the front lines of climate impacts and the delivery of essential services that make communities safer, healthier, and more resilient, yet too often lack the resources to respond. Cities and local communities especially need greater access to adaptation finance.

“It was disappointing to see no dedicated ocean event at the Leaders’ Summit, despite over 90% of countries including ocean action in national climate plans. The ocean is on the front lines of the climate crisis, but it could also be one of our greatest allies in tackling it. Ocean-based solutions can provide up to one-third of the emissions cuts needed by 2050 to keep 1.5°C within reach. This ambition for ocean action must be reflected in any COP31 cover decision and translate into concrete progress, especially for vulnerable coastal and island nations.

“Some leaders also delivered a resounding defense of multilateralism, even amid deep geopolitical tensions. International cooperation on climate may be changing shape, but it is still alive and needed now more than ever. Even in a fractured world, leaders recognize that no country can secure its economic future, build resilience, or prosper without working together on shared climate and environmental challenges. That spirit of cooperation must now carry through the negotiations and deliver a strong, ambitious outcome at COP31.”

WRI is a global research organization that spans more than 50 countries, with offices in Brazil, China, Europe, India, Indonesia, and the United States. Our more than 450 experts and staff work closely with leaders to turn big ideas into action to sustain our natural resources—the foundation of economic opportunity and human well-being. Find out more at www.wri.org

#5708. Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks

Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.

The startup's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports, labs and other largely unstructured information, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania Health goes beyond summarizing medical records; it uses AI to convert messy, unstructured clinical records into usable datasets and insights.

Nvidia provides the computing infrastructure needed to perform that analysis across potentially entire patient populations behind the hospital firewall, without transferring patient records outside the health system, according to the company.

Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise, while Nvidia brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises, Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, told Fierce Healthcare.

Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review, while keeping patient data inside the hospital’s own infrastructure, Schlosser said.

Health systems have vast amounts of valuable clinical information locked in unstructured medical records, but manually reviewing those records makes it difficult to use that data at scale for research, registries and predictive models. Synapsis AI aims to remove that bottleneck by analyzing patients’ records longitudinally, determining what happened and when, and identifying the clinical evidence supporting those conclusions, according to the company, which launched out of stealth two years ago.

Frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but the architectures, training data sets, as well as logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment, Schlosser noted.

Dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning. This specialized approach is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model, Schlosser asserted.

"Every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results, and for the first time we can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time,” Schlosser said.

Synapsis AI is built on the Nvidia AI enterprise software stack end to end. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the Nvidia NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.

Hospitals can use their own historical patient data to determine which treatments work for which patients, identify care gaps and ultimately recommend the next appropriate action, according to Schlosser.

Under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on Nvidia infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with Nvidia's healthcare software stack. The companies are exploring additional Nvidia technologies to secure AI processing, handle multiple clinical workloads at once and scale computing capacity, with the goal of moving from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insights at the point of care.

"Health systems need AI they can trust, integrate into their workflows and operate efficiently. That means connecting information across clinical systems, validating performance for the patients they serve, protecting sensitive data and making results useful within the tools clinicians already use," Chelsea Sumner, Nvidia's U.S. healthcare AI startups ecosystem lead, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Dyania’s approach addresses part of that challenge by running inside the hospital’s own environment and linking findings to evidence in the patient record. Scaling also requires clinicians, technology teams and hospital leaders to work together from the start, with clear responsibility for reviewing results and monitoring performance. Success should be measured by whether AI helps teams find patients who need attention, make better-informed decisions and spend more time delivering care," Sumner said.

Cleveland Clinic used Dyania Health’s Synapsis AI, running on Nvidia infrastructure, to analyze up to 16 years of records from 7,812 aortic valve replacement patients. The study addressed a central concern for patients: How long will the replacement valve last, and will another procedure be needed?

Researchers reviewed nearly 8,000 patient records between 2005 and 2021, mostly narrative notes and echocardiogram reports that registries can struggle to capture.

"Understanding how a replacement heart valve performs means following a patient across years of care, connecting the original operative report with subsequent progress notes, hospitalizations, echocardiograms, other medical conditions and later interventions. Much of that information is buried in narrative records that researchers would otherwise need to review manually," Schlosser noted.

The AI extracted information from narrative clinical records and answered 88 questions per patient about their valves, health conditions and subsequent care. Each answer linked to supporting evidence in the chart, he noted.

Researchers used that dataset to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and the risk of another intervention. The model estimates valve deterioration and repeat-procedure risk at three, five and 10 years post-procedure, with estimates that update as new medical information about the patient becomes available.

"Historically, this would have required human manual abstraction, and for 7,812 patients, it would be humanly impossible to read and abstract features on an ongoing basis at the rate at which medical records are changing. Additionally, humans reading a medical record can often miss information if they skim through it," Schlosser said.

The tool is used to help inform care but requires external validation from clinicians.

"Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients," said Lars G. Svensson, M.D., Ph.D., chief of the Heart, Vascular and Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic, in a statement.

The health system began working with Dyania Health a year ago to use its AI platform for clinical trial recruitment.

Synapsis AI made it possible for the first time to comprehensively analyze nearly two decades of patient data, Schlosser asserted. "What was even more groundbreaking was the ability to go from raw data in unstructured form to predictive risk models in one fell swoop. This enables precision care at scale and empowers physicians with stronger sets of information backing their clinical decisions about any given patient, including questions like 'when should the patient have their next echo?' or 'when will the patient likely need a reintervention?'" Schlosser said.

The Cleveland Clinic and Dyania Health collaboration reflects Nvidia's broader focus to provide healthcare and life sciences innovators with the computing platform and AI tools to advance research and help care teams better understand patients’ needs, Sumner said.

The heart valve study shows how Synapsis AI could help health systems use their own patient data to determine which treatments work best for which patients and improve predictive models over time, ultimately supporting more personalized care recommendations, according to Dyania Health.

"Nvidia's infrastructure enables us to handle more work concurrently and use resources more efficiently. That could allow hospitals to examine larger populations, ask more detailed questions and revisit analyses more frequently. The longer-term opportunity is to move from periodic batches of records toward insights available closer to the moment a clinician needs them," Schlosser said.

"We can do that within the health system’s own environment, keeping patient records behind its firewall. We are also evaluating capabilities for distributed inference, workload isolation and protection of data during computation. Computing power alone does not make a clinical conclusion correct; it allows a carefully developed clinical system to work at greater scale and speed," he said.

Sumner asserts that healthcare organizations are just scratching the surface on the potential for AI to uncover clinically useful information buried in longitudinal patient records.

"Connecting a physician’s notes with earlier test results and treatment history could help identify patients who need follow-up, match people with clinical trials and give researchers a clearer understanding of how treatments perform over time," she said. "The Cleveland Clinic heart valve study is a concrete example. AI helped researchers assemble a detailed view of patients’ care to study how replacement valves deteriorate. The opportunity is to turn that knowledge into more personalized monitoring and better-informed care decisions. Clinicians need to be able to review the supporting evidence, validate the findings and decide what they mean for each patient."

#5706. Industry Voices—From pledges to progress: Kill the clipboard, keep an eye on consistency

Industry Voices—From pledges to progress: Kill the clipboard, keep an eye on consistency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

For many patients, the clipboard remains one of healthcare’s most familiar frustrations.

At nearly every visit, patients are asked to provide information they have already supplied elsewhere, including their insurance coverage, medications, family history and previous surgeries. This repetitious hassle—even if managed on tablets as in recent years—frustrates patients, increases the risk of incomplete or inaccurate information entering the record, and takes unnecessary staff time to reconcile.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Health Technology Ecosystem initiative offers a compelling alternative through the Kill the Clipboard pledge. The effort is focused on moving technology and care practices forward so that patients can more easily retrieve and share their health information through personal health records or other health apps, removing the need for their data to be reconstructed at every encounter.

That shift could conclusively improve the patient experience. Reaching that goal, however, will require more than voluntary commitments from individual technology developers. This multi-stakeholder initiative needs work based on consensus-based standards, reliable infrastructure, clear data governance and careful attention to how new capabilities affect clinical work.

Patients often assume that health data interoperability is happening more than it is, and certainly more easily. In some cases, a person opens an app and shares their information with a provider themselves; in others, the exchange is initiated by their clinical care team. Behind that process, though, is a complex chain of care organizations, electronic health records (EHRs), identity verification services, intermediaries, standards development organizations, application developers and networks.

Consider, for example, real-time prescription benefit information. Giving patients cost and coverage options during an encounter—and ensuring that the information is accurate all the way to the point of sale—could help increase affordability and medication adherence. Yet the experience depends on pharmacy networks, price comparison apps and other third parties delivering complete, timely information into the clinician’s prescribing workflow, all while the patient is there in the exam room or awaiting discharge from the hospital. Every participant in the chain is fundamental to the increasingly complex web of health information exchange.

A 2025 study of more than 8,100 family physicians published in JAMA Network Open underscores just how much work around data-sharing remains. Depending on the type of clinical information, only 8% to 19% of survey respondents reported that outside data were routinely available, easy to find and easy to use within their EHRs.

Pledges like Kill the Clipboard can establish a valuable direction for the industry and encourage momentum. They will face challenges with adoption and impact, however, if sufficient effort doesn’t go into resolving dependencies across the country’s health tech ecosystem. Clear technical standards, realistic implementation timelines and ways to verify that promised capabilities work in practice are essential.

While the goals of increasing patient control over their own data, tackling inefficiencies, and increasing affordable care delivery are laudable and things no one would argue with, it is also true that moving quickly without those foundations could create expensive rework down the road or inadvertently widen the digital divide. If any or all pledge criteria eventually become certification requirements, as Dr. Tom Keane, the National Coordinator for Health IT, has intimated could be a possibility, the variability in readiness among different companies could become a problematic gap.

Expanding digital access also raises important questions about how patient data will be used once it leaves a regulated clinical environment.

There has been a huge proliferation of health apps in recent years intended to help patients more actively manage their own health while also better managing their medical records. Many can deliver meaningful value, but patients who are considering use of such an app need clearer information about whether an application may retain, combine, share or sell their data. Consent language should be understandable, with governance expectations following the information across the digital ecosystem, but the current legal and regulatory system needs modernization to ensure sufficient patient awareness.

Patient matching presents another safety concern. A larger volume of exchanged data is useful only when organizations can confidently connect each record to the correct person. Striking the right balance between the stringency of matching criteria and the goal of increasing data exchange is critical, as a clinician could make a prescribing or treatment decision based on another person’s medications, allergies, diagnoses or laboratory results with damaging consequences. Strong identity verification and thoughtful matching practices therefore belong at the center of any effort to make health data more portable, ensuring that patient safety protections are inherent to the matching process.

The potential consequences have recently been measured. A 2026 BMJ Quality & Safety study found that hospitalized patients with duplicate charts had 3.5 times the odds of requiring intensive care, 4.7 times the odds of inpatient death and hospital stays that were 32% longer than those of matched patients without duplicate charts. Although the observational study does not establish causation, it underscores the clinical risks associated with fragmented patient information.

For virtually any initiative focused on the patient, program vision and software design must also account for the people delivering care.

Primary care clinicians often have only a few minutes to review a patient’s record, conduct their initial assessment of the problem, complete documentation of the encounter, place orders and determine any necessary follow-up. While unquestionably helpful, adding review of new extensive patient data that has been sent from a patient’s medical record aggregation app adds another step that takes time. Then, needing to build in time to consider prescription cost comparisons, scheduling stemming from referrals, discussions of patient consent preferences, or record reconciliation further consumes part of a tightly constrained visit.

The impact on the provider and staff workflows in no way diminishes the value to the patient. These changes benefit all of us as patients and/or caregivers ourselves—but the implications for that workflow cannot be an afterthought.

The strongest implementations will embed new capabilities directly into existing workflows and surface information exactly when it is most useful. Software developers should also involve practicing clinicians in design, testing and governance so that any improvements support better care without introducing avoidable friction. In fact, prioritizing the efficient implementation of these new functionalities will increase adoption and user satisfaction, moving us all closer to our collective goals.

Eliminating the clipboard is the correct ambition, as are the goals of the other Health Tech Ecosystem pledges. They would serve patients nationwide and represent broader industry change in how we move and manage information. Patients should not have to recount their histories every time they seek care, and clinicians should have dependable data available whenever decisions must be made.

With mature standards, real-time connectivity, responsible governance, reliable patient matching and thoughtful workflow design, we can collectively turn the pledge’s aims into a new reality: more trusted digital experiences that give patients greater control and help everyone involved in their care act with greater confidence.

Leigh Burchell is vice president of policy and public affairs at Altera Digital Health, as well as chair of the Electronic Health Record Association.

#5705. Cummins Told Electrolyser Customers to Stop. Who Keeps the Hydrogen Plants Running?

Cummins is withdrawing from new electrolyser sales, but its customers have a problem that cannot be handled by closing a sales office. In September, its Hydrogenics subsidiaries recommended that customers stop using HyLYZER electrolysers following a review of operating data. The company disclosed the recommendation in its November quarterly report, said that it had not launched a recall, and was still assessing what modifications might be needed for equipment to return to service. It had not established the cost of resolving the issue and warned that the eventual financial effect could be material.

Cummins had a substantial position in the PEM electrolyser business. Accelera reports more than 45 HyLYZER 500 systems and more than 20 HyLYZER 1000 systems rated at 5 MW each. Using those minimum reported system counts and equipment ratings, its historical deployments represent roughly 145–213 MW, equivalent to 11–16% of the IEA’s projected 1.3 GW global PEM installed base at the end of 2026. Cummins has not published the number of HyLYZER plants covered by its September recommendation. The company is leaving a sizeable equipment estate requiring expert maintenance, field engineers and potential safety modifications.

The timing makes the situation consequential. Cummins announced in February that it intended to cease new commercial electrolyser activity, while continuing existing customer commitments. Its 2025 Accelera restructuring and impairment charges reached $458 million across several actions, including the electrolyser retreat. It is reducing specialist capacity at the same time as installed equipment needs engineering attention. Revenue from new orders can disappear faster than warranties, service obligations and safety responsibilities.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing on Cummins’ hydrogen hangover examines the HyLYZER warning, the customer projects and the financial implications of manufacturers leaving shrinking markets. The underlying evidence and project comparisons are in the full analysis.

The problem now moves from selling hardware to keeping it safe and serviceable. Investigating field data, testing modifications, certifying repair procedures and maintaining proprietary controls requires specialist teams. Those teams must remain capable long after the sales pipeline and the business unit built around it have contracted.

Estonia’s Stargate Hydrogen has taken over Cummins’ legacy HySTAT alkaline electrolyser platform and supplies replacement stacks and service for a fleet of more than 400 installations. That handover shows how intellectual property, manufacturing capability and field-service expertise can survive an OEM exit. Cummins’ HyLYZER PEM fleet needs its own engineering and aftermarket solution.

For owners, the financial question also depends on the purpose of the hydrogen. Air Liquide’s 20 MW Bécancour installation and Linde’s 35 MW Niagara Falls project serve companies with industrial hydrogen customers and alternative supply networks. Interruptions can mean lost sales, replacement purchases and costs of maintaining customer commitments. An owner with contracted industrial demand has a commercial reason to restore production, provided the equipment can meet the required safety standards and the replacement supply costs justify it.

Florida Power & Light’s Cavendish project presents another decision. Its 25 MW HyLYZER installation converts electricity to hydrogen for limited blending into natural gas used in power generation. Even without a stop-use issue, that application has to compete with using electricity directly or obtaining reliable grid services by other means. At an illustrative 55 kWh/kg of electrolyser electricity and 60% combined-cycle generation efficiency, about 36% of the original electricity returns after converting it to hydrogen and burning it, before compression and storage. Input power at $50/MWh would cost roughly $138/MWh of recovered electricity before equipment and operating expenses. Repairing the electrolyser would not change that conversion arithmetic.

The economic difference appears again at Hysolar’s Nieuwegein installation. A 2025 KWR H-Flex evaluation documented project delays, higher costs and hydrogen demand expanding more slowly than planned. Its electrolyser, dedicated pipeline, refuelling station and vehicle customers are linked by a common demand forecast. Better equipment performance helps only when enough customers will buy the hydrogen at prices covering production and delivery. The same distinction applies to demonstration projects combining buses, heating, electricity and gas blending: several proposed uses do not guarantee several profitable markets.

Manufacturers face the cost of retaining the people and intellectual property to support complex equipment long after the expected growth market has contracted. Cummins’ separate exit from its low-pressure fuel-cell business illustrates the potential bill: in March 2026, it made a $175 million net payment as part of a sale, cancellation of commitments and claims settlement, producing a $199 million accounting charge. Those are fuel-cell transaction figures, not estimated HyLYZER repair costs. The PEM matter remains unquantified.

The customers’ cost can exceed the repair bill. Owners need a safe restart route, long-term supply of stacks and controls, a price for replacement hydrogen during outages, and buyers able to pay for the output afterward. Lenders face a thinner resale market for specialised plants when their OEM leaves. Public funders face grant, regulated cost-recovery and guarantee liabilities when projects stop operating.

The wider hydrogen market makes these questions urgent. The IEA’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 finds that global demand still sits overwhelmingly in traditional industry and refining. Only about one-fifth of newly signed low-emissions hydrogen offtake volumes in 2025 had firm contractual commitments. A producer, refuelling-station operator and vehicle buyer can each invest on the assumption that the other two will grow. That is one demand risk distributed across three balance sheets, not three independent investments.

The next investment decision needs a safe route back to service, contracted customers, dependable parts supply and a costed exit alternative. Governments should direct support toward industrial customers who need hydrogen and can pay for it, rather than finance energy-carrier applications that lose to direct electricity. Cummins is exposing the long tail of earlier commitments. Other suppliers, buyers and lenders still control their next decisions.

The complete Cummins analysis compares industrial-gas plants, fuel-substitution pilots, refuelling systems and legacy equipment obligations. The earlier Cummins–Alstom assessment shows how similar service liabilities can persist in fuel-cell transportation.

#5704. A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease

A natural substance found in broccoli could offer an unexpected new approach to treating a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system. Researchers at Swinburne University have identified promising effects from the compound, raising hopes for a more affordable and accessible treatment for patients with few available options.

The disease, known as Friedreich ataxia, causes nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord to gradually deteriorate. As the damage progresses, patients lose their ability to coordinate movements, walk, and speak. The condition can also shorten life expectancy, and there is currently no cure. Approximately 200 Australians are living with the disease.

In a new study, scientists found that sulforaphane, a naturally occurring compound in broccoli, can increase levels of frataxin, a protein that is present in insufficient amounts in people with Friedreich ataxia. The researchers also found that the compound can help protect vulnerable nerve cells from damage.

How a Broccoli Compound Could Protect Nerve Cells

Frataxin plays an important role in keeping cells functioning properly, particularly those with high energy demands, such as nerve cells. In Friedreich ataxia, a genetic defect leads to reduced production of this essential protein, contributing to the progressive damage that characterizes the disease.

Sulforaphane appears promising because its potential benefits extend beyond increasing frataxin levels. Research indicates that it can also influence several biological processes involved in disease progression, including cellular stress and inflammation. Addressing multiple sources of damage at once could make the compound a valuable candidate for further investigation.

The findings are particularly encouraging for children with Friedreich ataxia. According to lead researcher Associate Professor Faith Kwa of Swinburne University, children account for a large proportion of those affected, yet no treatments specifically approved for pediatric patients are currently available.

"Friedreich ataxia is a devastating rare genetic disease that progressively steals a child's ability to walk, speak, play, and ultimately survive," she says.

"This novel therapeutic agent can target the underlying cause of the disease, while delivering an affordable and accessible therapy worldwide, improving treatment opportunities for families affected by this life-limiting disease.

"This discovery brings us closer to a future where children with Friedreich ataxia experience a better quality of life, greater independence, and an improved chance of long-term survival."

A Potential Treatment That Could Be More Accessible

One of the most encouraging aspects of sulforaphane is that it is not an entirely unfamiliar substance. The compound already has an established safety record in both children and adults, and purified, biologically active forms are commercially available.

These advantages could make it easier to develop a widely accessible treatment if future clinical trials confirm that sulforaphane is effective against Friedreich ataxia. However, further research is essential before scientists can determine whether the promising findings will translate into meaningful benefits for patients.

Kwa explains that the rarity of Friedreich ataxia creates additional challenges for researchers. Because relatively few people have the disease, public awareness is limited, making it more difficult to attract the funding needed to investigate potential treatments.

Researchers Seek Funding for Clinical Trials

The Swinburne team hopes to secure financial support for clinical trials that would examine whether sulforaphane can deliver the same promising effects in people living with the disease.

"We are hoping to gain funding to conduct clinical trials and further prove the positive impact the broccoli compound could have on those suffering from Friedreich ataxia," she says.

"Sulforaphane already has an established safety record in children and adults, and its pure and bioactive form is commercially available. This means if clinical trials prove successful, its rollout could accelerate the path to patient impact."

For patients and families facing a progressive illness with no cure, even improvements in everyday functioning and independence could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their work will not only advance treatment possibilities but also bring greater attention to a condition that remains largely unknown to the public.

"Even if we can raise awareness of this debilitating condition or improve one person's quality of life, our efforts will have been worth it."

Materials provided by Swinburne University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5703. Energy Drink's Surprising Ingredient Likely Sparked Severe Reaction

— The drink contained fish collagen, which may be an under-recognized allergen

A 15-year-old boy with eczema, asthma, idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis, and allergic rhinitis developed widespread hives, wheezing, and difficulty breathing within minutes of trying a new energy drink.

The energy drink contained 5 grams of fish collagen derived from cod, which is suspected to be the culprit behind the teen's anaphylaxis, reported Annabelle Rowland, MD, a resident physician at the Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology (ACAAI) 2026 Annual Scientific Meeting in Phoenix.

The patient first presented to the emergency department where he was treated with two doses of intramuscular epinephrine as well as albuterol, cetirizine, and isotonic fluids until his symptoms subsided. He told doctors that he was in his usual state of health earlier that day and hadn't exercised or taken nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

In the past, the teen had noticed mild throat itching and lip swelling when he ate canned tuna, but he was able to eat salmon with no issues. He reported tolerating the "big 9" allergens. Of note, the patient developed localized hives after previous exposure to chlorhexidine wash.

After the emergency department, the teen had skin prick testing in the allergy clinic. He was negative for tuna, cod, and flounder but positive for environmental allergens. Rowland noted the patient's working diagnosis is an allergy to fish collagen, though the patient was lost to follow-up, and therefore confirmatory with testing with fresh cod was not done.

"Standard fish allergy tests mostly look for a different fish protein and contain very little collagen, so a person can test negative and still react," Rowland told MedPage Today. She explained that most commercially available serum testing for fish allergy is parvalbumin-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE), whereas "fish collagen is a cross-reactive protein across multiple fish species."

She noted that some studies have shown that most patients who are sensitized to parvalbumin are also sensitized to fish collagen, but there was a small subset of patients who only showed sensitization to the latter. Other research has demonstrated that some fish-allergic patients may have significant symptoms to as little as 1 mg of protein.

Fish collagen is not water-soluble and may not be present in sufficient amounts to elicit a positive test from standardized skin-prick extracts, the researchers noted. Thus, patients with fish collagen allergy may be at risk for false-negative testing with both standard serum and skin-prick tests.

"This case shows how tricky fish allergy can be," Rowland said in a press release, adding that fish-based collagen is popping up in a growing number of foods and supplements.

Rowland said the takeaway is that it's important to read ingredient labels closely as more unexpected protein sources are added to products.

Zachary Rubin, MD, a pediatric allergist who practices near Chicago, told MedPage Today that most would not associate energy drinks with fish allergens, but with fish-derived collagen popping up in drinks, supplements, and more, there are increased opportunities for unexpected exposure.

To Rubin, this case illustrates that "allergists sometimes need to investigate ingredients that might not be immediately obvious" and that "a negative standard allergy test doesn't always tell the whole story."

#5702. 7 Concerning And Strange Items From Real GM Service Bulletins

Have you been looking for some new reading material, something amusing, maybe strange, or even alarming? Have you thought about perusing automotive service bulletins? Probably not. But we're a bunch of incurable car nerds here at Jalopnik, so service announcements are exactly the kind of thing we might read over our morning bowl of Cheerios.

It turns out there's some entertaining — and sometimes surprisingly concerning — stuff in those bulletins. For example, did you know that a little nest of spiders could cause $300 worth of damage in some Chevy vehicles? That's not all. Some General Motors (GM) vehicles repeatedly prank-called OnStar for a while, and it turns out that the rugged full-size 2024 and 2025 Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra were no match for car washes. You might also be surprised to learn that safety features like airbags and automatic emergency brakes can turn on you, and that a leaky roof can cause your key fob to stop working — and then there are all of the strange noises and odors.

You might expect some new cars to have problems or bugs that need to be corrected under warranty — maybe a transmission that doesn't shift right, some early coolant leaks, or a leaky sunroof. One thing you don't expect from a new car is it making prank calls to OnStar. Yet, according to one GM service update for the 2007 GMC Sierra, certain 2001-2008 light-duty trucks, Hummers, and even Saabs were exhibiting a "condition to which the vehicle owner/operator would be unaware of resulting in repeated incomplete calls to the OnStar being made." So, maybe instead of prank calling, it's more accurate to say the vehicles were doing the automotive electronic equivalent of butt dialing. The solution was a recall where the dealer would replace the OnStar Module (VCIM).

GM had acknowledged similar problems in an earlier service bulletin for the 2006 GMC Canyon, applicable to 1996 through 2008 OnStar-equipped vehicles, but the company mostly blamed the problem on customers. One explanation involved the customer hitting the white button, followed by the system misinterpreting a random sound, or background noise such as a "cough," as an emergency. Really, a cough? What would it do in case of a loud sneeze? Deploy the airbags?

Listen, people, you've got to take care of your trucks. That means not doing recklessly negligent things like washing them. At one point, drivers of some 2024 and 2025 Sierra/Silverado 2500 HDs and 3500 HDs found their check engine lights were coming on. Dealership technicians would see that the trucks were kicking out a DTC P244B diagnostic code, or "Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High Bank 1." The culprit? According to Bulletin No. PIP6020A (PDF), "Engineering has found that this code may set if the vehicle was recently washed."

But that's not the only way water has vexed GM vehicle owners. Some owners of 2021 Chevy Tahoes and GMC Yukons were hearing "gurgling noises" after heavy rains and, you guessed it, car washes. It turned out to be residual water in sunroof drain tubes. The fix was to turn on the HVAC blower in fresh air mode to blow out the remaining water.

At first, the Cybertruck was the only truck that would get messed up by car washes, as the simple act of taking a Cybertruck through a car wash could brick it and possibly void its warranty. GM followed suit, though the worst its trucks could muster was a measly check engine light.

Modern cars come with lots of safety features to help you avoid accidents. Unfortunately, those safety features can sometimes go rogue. The Cadillac XT4 comes equipped with automatic emergency braking, which will stop the car if it detects an obstacle before the driver sees it. We imagine it's probably prevented more than one distracted driver from rear-ending a stopped car. That's all well and good until the car starts coming to a halt for objects that aren't there. That's exactly what some 2024 XT4s were doing, as reported by Service Bulletin 24-NA-053 (PDF). Yikes.

We'd hate to have that happen to us when we're trying to merge onto the freeway while everyone else is going 80 mph. The bulletin said the cause "may" be limitations in the camera. The confidence conveyed there is very reassuring. Of course, that's not as scary as the time GM recalled several cars due to temporary loss of braking.

In a similar case, Program Bulletin 12084 (PDF) alerted dealers that the Sensing and Diagnostic Module on some 2013 Chevy Malibus could reset itself after a hard braking event, a process that lasted three seconds. If the driver were to execute an "aggressive" turning maneuver during those three seconds, the side airbags could deploy. Or, if there was an accident during those three seconds, the seatbelt pretensioner might not work. These scenarios seem oddly specific, causing us to think that maybe this actually happened more than once.

Everyone knows that one friend who is, shall we say, "hygiene-challenged" and would benefit from a good shower. Perhaps among carmakers, GM is that friend, considering how many service bulletins have to do with odd smells emanating from their vehicles. These odors range from annoying to downright alarming.

For example, one GM Bulletin addressed gear oil smell in vehicles with remote vents. On the dangerous side, one safety recall of the Buick Regal GS and Pontiac Grand Prix said that owners may notice a burning smell, indicating a fire under the hood. Drivers of several 2022-2024 GM models noticed a smoke smell coming from under their seats, and technicians were likely to find "melted burn marks around the height adjuster motor."

Meanwhile, one GM bulletin treated unwanted odors as a sales opportunity for its proprietary product, GM Vehicle Care Odor Eliminator. It pitched it to the dealerships to be used by their service center techs for detailing as well as prepping their used cars for sale. To be fair, some smells can make a car hard to sell. It suggested that the product be given as a gift with a new car sale, as in, "Here's a little something for those unpleasant odors that will inevitably plague your new car." According to GM, displaying it prominently for sale would "increase dealership traffic" since the product isn't sold in stores. Sure, we can see people beating down the door to get their bottle of GM Vehicle Care Odor Eliminator.

Who doesn't like to hear a low growl that comes out of a powerful internal combustion engine? It's disturbing, though, to hear a growl when you put the car in park, whether the engine is running or not, but drivers of certain 1980 Oldsmobile Ninety Eights were hearing a growl when they would park the car on an incline. The GM bulletin that addressed this directed that drivers be told to engage the parking brake before shifting into park, then make sure the car is really in park.

What is the opposite of a growl? Chirps and squeaks might make good candidates. Those are the noises that have been coming out of some 2019-2023 model full-size trucks and SUVs. If we buy a full-size pickup with a huge V8, chirps and squeaks are not the kind of noises we want to hear coming from the engine. According to Bulletin 26-NA-021, ticks, taps, and typewriter noises have been heard coming from 2019 – 2026 Trucks. That has to be disconcerting.

Meanwhile, Bulletin 14-06-04-004G said that GM vehicles equipped with a two-stage vane-type oil pump have been known to make "Rrrrp" or "Rasp" noises when the engine starts in freezing weather or if the engine has been sitting for a few hours. Even weirder, the same bulletin said that vehicles equipped with a 6.2-liter engine may let out a "moan" after a cold start, at idle, or during operation at low RPMs. What's really weird is that GM says that all of these noises are normal.

Key fobs stop working from time to time. When it happens to us, we order a new battery from Amazon and call it a day. However, it has never occurred to us to check the car's roof. GM Service Bulletin 23-NA-107 (PDF) addressed pinhole leaks that would sometimes occur in the 2024 Chevy Trax. Oddly enough, that could cause the key fob to stop working. Apparently, water would get into some of the electronics, which somehow impacted the connection with the key fob. We have to give kudos to the engineer or technician who put two and two together and figured this out.

Key fobs don't have to be malfunctioning to help with troubleshooting, though. Some owners of the 2023 Cadillac XT4 and 2024 and 2025 Buick Envision had complained that the lights would flash when the vehicle was parked and the battery would be drained until it died. GM said this was likely caused by a defect in the K171 Rear Closure Hands Free Module. How could the tech tell for sure that this was the cause? Easy. The bulletin said to tape the key fob to the rear wiper. If the rear gate opens when the lights flash, it must be the K171 Rear Closure Hands Free Module. Again, we marvel at the mind that was able to connect the dots in this way.

No one likes to see the check engine light come on, but it was showing up on the dashboards of certain Buick Encore, Chevy Trax, and Chevy Sonic models during the 2010s for a surprising reason. Those vehicles were kicking out P0446 or P0455 error codes, indicating a restriction in the EVAP canister. Inconvenient, sure, but not strange — except that the service bulletin instructed technicians to check the EVAP canister for spider nests. We don't know why spiders liked this part so much or how many times techs found spiders in these EVAP canisters before this bulletin was put out, but apparently it happened enough for GM to rule arachnids as the likely cause.

You'd think that the remedy would just be to evict the spiders from the EVAP canister. Nope. GM said that the entire EVAP canister would need to be replaced. That's a $300 part. Who knew that a nest of spiders could do so much damage?

You might not think it, but service bulletins can make for an entertaining read, and we've just skimmed the surface with the examples we've covered here. If you're bored, you can check out more GM bulletins on the company's official website, and let us know in the comments if you come across any gems you find interesting.

#5701. Patient experience has improved across the healthcare industry. Now comes consistency

Patient experience has improved across the healthcare industry. Now comes consistency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient experience metrics collected over millions of encounters show continuous topline improvements across all types of care settings, either meeting or surpassing those reported ahead of the pandemic.

But the gains aren’t uniform, with substantial variation between organizations, regions, patient groups, admission types, specialty and other operational factors under providers’ control, warned Qualtrics in its “State of Patient Experience 2026” report, released Thursday.

“The national trend-line is encouraging, but tells an incomplete story,” the report reads. “Some organizations are improving rapidly; others are standing still.”

The experience management software vendor’s analysis, released Thursday, pulled data from 43.1 million of its over 2,500 hospitals and 490,000 medical office site customers.

It showed that national patient experience scores like Likelihood to Recommend (LTR) reached new highs in ambulatory surgery (86 out of 100), medical practice (86), inpatient (70.5) and emergency department (69.5) settings through 2025. Overall ratings across each of those settings also improved from the prior year, with the exception of a slight decline (70.4 to 69.7) among inpatient facilities.

Several data points highlighted in the report paint a picture of how inconsistencies or other operational hurdles can impact patients’ reported experiences, and how providers with the best overall satisfaction scores stand out in those areas.

When comparing a planned versus an unplanned admission, for instance, hospitals in the top quartile of overall patient experience scores recorded an 8.9-point median gap between the two encounter types. At bottom-quartile hospitals, unplanned admissions were a median 18.2 points lower.

At the same time, practices that encourage consistent care delivery can make scores for unplanned visits look more like their counterparts. Here, the vendor pointed to bedside shifts, a nursing practice in which nurses going off duty update the on-duty nurse with patient care information at the bedside. A planned admission that did not have a bedside shift was tied to a 68.3 LTR, versus a 76.5 LTR during an unplanned admission that included a bedside shift.

That data point is also an example of the loyalty benefit providers can enjoy when implementing practices to address operational friction, described as a chief drag on patients’ likelihood to recommend a provider. In an inpatient setting, for instance, patients who reported no operational friction rewarded hospitals with LTR scores of 90.6, versus 60.3 when friction is present. These types of operational factors had a greater negative impact on experience scores than those related to clinical care, per Qualtrics’ data.

“The highest performing organizations double down on reliability and consistency, making exceptional experiences the standard, not the exception,” the report reads.

Another standout in the data was patients’ favorable responses to caregivers demonstrating teamwork and trust. Units in the top quartile for teamwork (where patients report “staff worked together for you”) were almost twice as likely to notch top hospital ratings, while those with high levels of trust (as reported by employees) are about 2.4 times as likely to be a top performer.

“Teamwork has emerged as the defining key driver of confidence in care and lasting loyalty,” the report reads. “Patients notice when caregivers communicate clearly, coordinate effectively, and work together toward a common goal.”

Qualtrics’ report concludes with several patient experience recommendations for organizations to target in the coming year. Among these are embracing omnichannel listening, or combining traditional metrics like survey data with other channels; reducing workforce administrative burden to maximize patient face time; and removing barriers that keep patients from making an appointment, including by reserving slots for first visits or by offering assisted scheduling.
